title: Excessive gas consumption in pool operations
body: In contracts/pair_concentrated_duality/src/execute.rs:148 , the provide_liquidity function allows users to supply liquidity to the pool. However, when order book integration is enabled, this operation becomes extremely gas-intensive, potentially leading to out-of-gas failures and block inefficiencies. This issue extends to all pool operations as they similarly depend on costly order book interactions, making them vulnerable to gas exhaustion and inefficient block execution. The execution flow for provide_liquidity includes, in the worst case where num_orders is equal to ORDER_SIZE_LIMITS.end() : 1. Performing 60 QuerySimulateCancelLimitOrderRequest queries to retrieve order states. 2. Processing cumulative trades, updating prices, and computing LP shares. 3. Queuing a mint message. 4. Queuing 60 MsgCancelLimitOrder and 60 MsgPlaceLimitOrder messages, and a callback to ReplyIds::PostLimitOrderCb . 5. The callback executes 60 additional QuerySimulateCancelLimitOrderRequest queries. Given Neutron's block.max_gas limit of 30,000,000 , the gas cost for a single liquidity provision can be estimated as: ● MsgPlaceLimitOrder ( good_till_completed ): 31,095 gas ● MsgCancelLimitOrder : 25,451 gas ● Total for 60 orders: 3,392,760 gas ● Additional costs: Queries, minting, callbacks, and computation. Consequently, the theoretical maximum is less than 8.84 provide_liquidity calls per block. An empirical test case defined in the Appendix describes the gas used per provide_liquidity call equal to 5,096,372 , resulting in a maximum of 5 provide_liquidity transactions per block. Since only five transactions fit within a block, the execution order depends on the mempool state. If a transaction is executed while less than 1/5 of block gas remains, it will likely fail due to insufficient gas or be directly discarded by the block proposer. This makes it impractical for 12 a basic action like providing liquidity to consume such a large portion of the block's resources, especially on a shared blockchain with multiple competing protocols. This inefficiency applies not only to provide_liquidity but to all pool operations as they all depend on canceling and registering orders in the order book. Recommendation We recommend reducing the number of messages and interactions with the order book to lower the gas costs of individual pool operations. As a short-term mitigation, we suggest limiting the maximum number of orders per side, which is currently set at 30 , to a lower value to improve efficiency and prevent excessive resource consumption. Status: Resolved

title: Disabling of Neutron order book causes pool operations failure
body: The Neutron order book is designed to allow governance to disable it, preventing the setting or cancellation of orders as the associated messages will fail and revert. However, since all pool operations rely on calling the cancel_orders function, disabling the Neutron orderbook results in the failure and reversion of all pool operations, rendering the pool non-functional. This issue also arises if the pool administrator tries to disable the order book integration. Specifically, the process_custom_msgs function in contracts/pair_concentrated_duality/src/execute.rs:693-727 will fail when the orderbook is disabled, as it invokes the cancel_orders function, which will revert. As a result, disabling the Neutron order book effectively locks the pool, even though it could otherwise function using its internal automated market maker logic. Recommendation We recommend decoupling pool operations from the orderbook's availability by implementing fallback mechanisms that allow the pool to continue functioning independently when the Neutron orderbook is disabled. Status: Acknowledged The client states that, with the current design, they cannot continue operations while a portion of their liquidity remains locked in the order book. 13 For example, if 50% of the liquidity is allocated to the order book, it would be frozen at outdated prices while the remaining liquidity is utilized in PCL. When the market resumes, these stale prices could disrupt the PCL repegging algorithm, potentially rendering it inoperable.

title: stakes vector could exceed the CosmWasm VM memory limit when loaded
body: In contracts/registry-stake/src/state.rs:68 , the stakes attribute is defined in the State struct as a vector of strings. This implies that every time the read_state function is invoked, all the State data, including the stakes vector, is loaded into memory. Since the stakes vector has no maximum length, the CosmWasm VM memory could not have enough space available to load it resulting in an execution panic. A bad actor could intentionally use this issue to cause any interaction with the protocol to be very gas intensive, up to the point where any interaction will run out of gas. With current parameters on Osmosis, the cost of this attack would be in the millions of US dollars. While this might still be economically viable, we classify this issue as major, since it can be resolved with a contract upgrade. 10 Recommendation We recommend defining a hard cap for stakes vector size or implementing a different data structure that gives access to the required information without loading the entire vector data in memory. Status: Resolved

title: Unstake transactions are likely to fail if more than one of them is processed in the same block
body: The Unstake transaction handler, defined in contracts/registry-stake/src/contract.rs:635-698 , takes as input parameter a vector of numeric indexes that represent the user's stake slots in the stakes vector. In order to process the deletion of the vector data at the provided indexes within an O(1) asymptotic cost, the swap_remove function is used. This method performs a delete substituting data in the selected index slot with the data stored in the latest element of the vector. Consequently, a removal of one element affects also the ordering of the elements stored in the latest positions of the vector. If we have more than one Unstake transaction in the same block, the indexes for any subsequent positions might be wrong, leading to an error, or, if the same sender controls the position, to the deletion of the wrong position. This implies that the likelihood of an Unstake transaction to succeed depends on different unpredictable factors like: ● The order of transactions in a block ● The cardinality of Unstake transactions in a block ● The distance of the index to the end of the stakes vector The likelihood of having a transaction error increases drastically on particular events, for example a market crash where users may want to exit funds from the protocol quickly. Additionally, bad actors can grieve users by staking many small amounts, and then front-running others to cause unstake failures. This could be used together with a short of the tokens to attack the whole protocol and profit from a panic in users. 11 Recommendation We recommend collecting all the indexes that have to be deleted from different Unstake transactions and then remove them when electing the next epoch executor . Another solution could be using a tree, for example an avl::AvlTreeMap in order to store new positions. Status: Acknowledged

title: Protocol is prone to censorship
body: The guard defined in contracts/registry-stake/src/contract.rs:342-347 ensures that only the currently elected executor can submit the ExecuteRequest message. This implies that if the currently elected executor is not responsive and actively participating, the protocol will be stuck for the entire epoch with no executed requests . Since every AUTO token holder can stake its tokens and participate in the election, there is a possibility that the executor could be an inactive protocol participant. Also, a malicious actor could stake a large amount of tokens in order to intentionally stop the requests execution, causing all or targeted executions to get delayed. This is particularly impactful for users and attractive for attackers if requests contain trading transactions that require to be executed in a timely manner. Usually, in proof of stake (PoS) systems, such actors would bear an economic cost such as infrastructure maintenance, cost of staked capital, and third-party delegation loss. Also, in this case, it is required to deposit the stake in the contract only for one block since there is no unbonding period, reducing the attacker's capital cost and making the attack cheaper with respect to other PoS systems. In fact, in contracts/registry-stake/src/contract.rs:635-698 , the Unstake message handler allows the currently elected executor to unstake all of its stake slots without losing its role. Consequently the executor can be in charge of its role without having its stake deposited in the protocol. This would allow an attacker to get an AUTO loan, stake and be elected, unstake, repay the loan and act as an inactive executor in order to stop requests execution without having to hold or loan tokens for long. Also, it is worth to note that in contracts/registry-stake/src/contract.rs:645 , during the handling of the Unstake transaction, the executor election is done before removing the unstaking user's address from the stakes vector. This implies that an 12 unstaking user could be elected as the current epoch executor without having capital at risk stored in protocol. We classify this issue as minor since the client intends to set the epoch length to 100 blocks, which corresponds to 10 minutes on Osmosis and is low enough to reduce the impact of an attack. Still, market manipulation even over a short time window may be exploited. Recommendation We recommend: a) Increasing the cost for an executor by disallowing executors to unstake while they are elected. b) Increasing the cost for an executor by adding an unbonding period. c) Keeping the epoch duration short to reduce the amount of damage an inactive executor can cause. d) Increasing the number of executors per epoch, such that there is no single point of failure. Multiple executors could be allowed to execute requests within alternating preassigned slots. This prevents inactive executors to block the protocol, since there are multiple ones in each epoch, so requests are still executed. While there are multiple approaches, executor selection could be done by randomly choosing from the set of stake-weighted executors, while removing already selected executors to prevent double-selection. In the next epoch, the same algorithm should run again, without filtering out previously selected executors. For an efficient implementation, an optimized data structure should be used, for example, a sortition sum tree. Status: Acknowledged The client states: tl;dr there is actually infact no additional cost to attack Autonomy compared to any other PoS system with a similar market cap. The recommendations don't actually solve the underlying issues, which are present in every other PoS system such as ETH. c) is valid in that the recommendation would marginally help (but not solve) the underlying issue, but the difference in practicality between other PoS systems and Autonomy in regard to c) are so small that it likely wouldn't actually make a difference to the decision to attack, and the 2nd order effects of implementing the recommendation could cause more harm than the underlying issue it's trying to prevent. It's true an executor has the ability to censor or ignore txs to the exact same degree as a validator/miner in any PoS/PoW etc system - this is a widely known and acknowledged issue with any consensus protocol/blockchain. As with other PoS/PoW etc systems, the attacker is losing out in fee revenue by censoring things and therefore pays an opportunity cost, and the requests will eventually be executed aslong as there is atleast 1 executor who is purely financially motivated / not malicious. There is no extra ability of an attacker to do this in Autonomy vs any other system like ETH's PoS etc. It's true that performing the censorship attack on Autonomy doesn't require running infrastructure (bot/node) like it would in the ETH example, since you would still have to produce blocks which requires running an ETH node, but this cost, especially in comparison to the 13 amount of capital required to perform a censorship attack on Autonomy, is so small that it's a negligible rounding error and can basically be ignored. Presumably 'cost of staked capital' is referring to the loss in value of the staked AUTO tokens when performing the censorship attack - an attacker's optimal strategy is to borrow AUTO tokens and use them to stake, since they only need to repay the debt in AUTO and therefore don't suffer a loss from any price decrease in AUTO when censoring. This is equally possible in ETH - to borrow ETH with stablecoins as collateral, stake it, produce empty blocks in an attempt to drop the price of ETH, and not lose any money because the debt is denominated in ETH. An unbonding/unstaking period does not change the economics of this attack. It is therefore not cheaper to perform the censorship attack on Autonomy vs a PoS system like ETH if it had an equivalent market cap to Autonomy. It's not a problem that executors can unstake while still being an executor because there is no slashing in the system (as it's impossible to prove malicious censorship, the same as it's not possible to slash for that in ETH or any other chain), and censoring is the only 'bad' thing that an executor can do. Recommendation responses: a) preventing unstaking while an executor/validator in any PoS system, including Autonomy, does not increase the cost of attack via devaluing of staked capital, if the attacker borrowed the tokens they staked, as shown above b) adding an unbonding period to any PoS system, including Autonomy, does not increase the cost of attack via devaluing of staked capital, if the attacker borrowed the tokens they staked, as shown above c) reducing the epoch length/time would not reduce an attacker's ability to censor in general because having 50% of the stake means they can only execute for 50% of the time, regardless of the epoch length. However it is true that, because of The Law of Large Numbers, a longer epoch means fewer epochs over a given (short in practicality) time period, which means there is a higher change that the same executor will be chosen for every epoch in that time period without interruption. However, e.g. on Osmosis the block time is ~6s, so 100 blocks is 600s i.e. 10 minutes. Assuming there is $100M of AUTO staked on Autonomy then in order for an executor to get 75% of the stake, they'd need to borrow $300M of AUTO and put up >> $300M as collateral. Then they have a 0.75^6 = 0.178% chance to be the executor for any given hour. The chance to censor for 1 full day is 0.75^(6*24) = 0.000000000000000001%. Therefore the chance of being able to fully censor for any amount of time that would cause the price of AUTO to dump is impractically low, especially given the capital requirements. It is true that even if an attacker isn't able to fully censor for an hour, simply causing delays in things like limit orders could impact the price of AUTO. There is an inherent tradeoff between the length of the epoch and the fees charged to users - the extreme of 1 epoch = 1 block would mean that executors would only be able to know whether they're executors for the next block, and would need to broadcast all their execution txs in the hope that they get added into the next block. The practical reality of blockchains is that this is rarely the case, and even using a 'fast' gas price results in the tx being mined >=2 block in the future. Therefore every executor would waste gas on most of their execution attempts that are reverted if they're mined after the next block when they're no longer the executor. This means that running an executor is now not guaranteed to be risk-free profitable, which it should be when not being malicious - the execution fee that goes to executors would therefore need to be increased in proportion to the risk of late-mined txs that comes with a smaller epoch length, increasing the cost and reducing the appeal of the system as a whole, leading to lower executor revenue overall. title: Malicious vote extensions can arbitrarily mutate bridge state after late precommit injection
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/abci/proposal.go:257-270 , the computeCA function that feeds the block proposal selects the vote extension from ci.Votes[0] without validating the payload. CometBFT sorts these votes by descending voting power, so the first entry belongs to the validator with the largest stake. Late precommits from prior heights bypass the application's VerifyVoteExtension hook, allowing a Byzantine top-power validator to broadcast a forged vote extension after the block is decided. The proposer will decode it, treat its IntentData as canonical, and insert the resulting transaction into the block. Subsequently, the pre-block handler executes those packets via the keeper.ExecuteVE function, implemented in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/ve_exec.go:56-188 without any verification, directly mutating RequestForFunds , PendingSettlement , and related bridge state. This enables arbitrary cross-chain settlements or price updates to be forged and committed, compromising the bridge's integrity. The impact is critical as funds can be misdirected or accounting corrupted without needing a majority coalition. Recommendation We recommend validating vote extensions during proposal construction. Specifically: ● Ensure the baseapp.ValidateVoteExtensions function is called before consuming the commit. ● Iterate over all ExtendedCommitInfo entries, skip non- BlockIDFlagCommit votes, and run the same checks performed in VerifyVoteExtensionHandler , rejecting any vote whose intents fail validation. ● Only aggregate intents that pass validation and require consensus (for example, ≥2/3 of voting power submitting an identical payload) before injecting the transaction. ● If no validated payload exists, avoid appending the synthetic transaction so a malicious validator cannot force arbitrary state changes. Status: Resolved 14

title: ProcessProposal accepts all proposals without validating vote extensions
body: The ProcessProposal function in xarachain:x/chainabstraction/abci/proposal.go:71-102 has all validation logic commented out and unconditionally accepts all proposals. This allows a malicious proposer to inject fake vote extension events ( DepositVEPacket , FulfilmentVEPacket ) that never occurred on external chains, manipulate ExtendedCommitInfo , and potentially drain funds by creating fake cross-chain events. The commented code includes critical validation via baseapp.ValidateVoteExtensions that verifies vote extensions are properly signed by validators and match the ExtendedCommitInfo . Without this validation, the bridge's security model is compromised as vote extensions serve as the source of truth for cross-chain events. Recommendation We recommend uncommenting and implementing the validation logic, including calling baseapp.ValidateVoteExtensions to verify vote extensions are cryptographically signed and match what validators actually committed to. Status: Resolved

title: Non-deterministic time check causes consensus failures
body: In the RefundReq function in xarachain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_refund_req.go:29 , the code uses time.Now() to check if a request for funds has expired. This creates non-determinism because each validator will see a different current time based on their system clock, which can differ by milliseconds or seconds. When validators execute the same transaction at different time.Now() values, they may reach different conclusions about whether the RFF has expired, causing consensus failures in which the transaction is accepted by some validators and rejected by others. This breaks the fundamental requirement that all validators must execute transactions deterministically and agree on the results. The chain may halt, or transactions may fail intermittently, depending on which validators process them first. Recommendation We recommend replacing time.Now() with ctx.BlockTime() , which provides the deterministic block time that all validators agree on. Status: Resolved 15

title: Only the latest 100 settlements are retrieved without marking them as completed, which prevents processing earlier settlements
body: In ca-node:vservice/settlement_ev.go:44-49 of the handleNewBlockActual function, the settlement polling mechanism requests settlements with a Limit of 100 and sets Reverse to true , which instructs the Cosmos query to return the newest 100 settlements first. Because the Cosmos SDK stores all settlements without marking processed ones as succeeded, the node repeats the same batch of recent entries on every iteration rather than advancing to older ones. Older settlements will therefore remain unhandled indefinitely, blocking the settlement pipeline. Recommendation We recommend fetching settlements in chronological order so that the oldest unprocessed items are handled first and marking processed settlements as completed to prevent reprocessing. Status: Acknowledged The client notes that it will be addressed as part of broader rearchitecting efforts planned for the system.

title: Refund logic allows already fulfilled requests to be reimbursed, allowing double spends and prematurely refunded deposits, resulting in locked liquidity
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_refund_req.go:14-66 , the RefundReq message handler returns the deposited assets once the request-for-funds (rff) has expired. The handler relies on the rff.Fulfilled flag in line 33 to reject refunds that have already been satisfied. However, the flag is populated by the vote-extension pipeline, which updates the chain state only after it observes the fulfillment transaction on the external destination chain. When the fulfillment transaction is executed shortly before expiry, there is a critical time window in which the external chain has already paid out the request, but rff.Fulfille d has not been set to true . During that window, the requester can call RefundReq to reclaim the deposited funds, receiving both fulfillment on the external chain and a refund from the vault. This enables a double-spend of the bridge's liquidity, resulting in a direct loss of funds. 16 Similarly, when the RFF expired without a successful fulfillment, the message handler refunds deposits on the source chain that were observed as RFFSourceState_DEPOSITED . If all deposits have been executed on the source chains but validators have not yet reached consensus via vote extension across all of them, the handler refunds all confirmed deposits and leaves the unconfirmed deposit locked in the vault. Because rff.Refunded becomes true , the request cannot be retried, and the liquidity remains stranded. The combined effect results in losses from double refunds and permanently locked liquidity whenever on-chain activity lags behind verification. Recommendation We recommend ensuring that refunds are processed only after the protocol has deterministically confirmed whether the RFF deposits and fulfillment succeeded or failed. Possible mitigations include tracking request-for-funds in transit and requiring additional confirmation before issuing refunds, or implementing a longer delay between fulfillment and expiry to allow state synchronization across chains. Status: Partially Resolved The client notes that the current 2-minute delay is a known configuration that will remain in place for the time being. It will be revisited as part of broader rearchitecting efforts planned for the system.

title: Unvalidated RFF publication enables P2P network spam and resource exhaustion
body: In the publishRFFToNewRequestsTopic function in vservice/rff.go:171-186 , RFF IDs are published to the P2P network without validation. The function accepts any RFF ID and publishes it to the GossipSub topic without verifying whether the RFF exists on-chain, is valid, or has already been fulfilled. While solvers validate the RFF's existence after receiving the message, the issue occurs during propagation: each message is broadcast to all P2P peers, consuming network bandwidth, flooding message queues, and triggering processing on every solver node. Even with early validation, each solver must perform Cosmos queries and spawn goroutines to verify the RFF, consuming computational and network resources. An attacker can spam arbitrary RFF IDs to exhaust P2P network resources, overwhelm solver nodes, consume the CA service's gas tokens during RFF processing, and potentially cause denial-of-service for legitimate RFF processing. 17 Recommendation We recommend validating RFF IDs before publishing by checking on-chain existence, fulfillment status, and expiry. Additionally, implement rate limiting, authentication, and duplicate detection to prevent abuse. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that VSCs will handle rate-limiting at the HTTP layer via a reverse proxy. They further clarify that since the P2P mesh is inherently open to the public and allows anyone to publish messages to the topic, rate-limiting the /api/v1/publish-rff endpoint alone would not provide meaningful protection against abuse.

title: Unbounded pending settlements are processed during the PreBlocker , which can cause consensus delays
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/abci/proposal.go:168-230 , the PreBlocker function calls keeper.GetAllPendingSettlement every SettlementInterval and aggregates every pending settlement entry into a settlement struct before re-enqueuing them through keeper.AppendSettlement . However, the pending settlements are unbounded. If there are many pending settlements, a proposer must process them, which can take considerable time and potentially exceed block timeouts, delaying block production. Recommendation We recommend enforcing a hard upper bound or a batching mechanism on pending settlements per interval (e.g., by limiting queue length, rate-limiting settlement creation, or processing settlements across multiple blocks) so that PrepareProposal cannot be forced to iterate over an unbounded set. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that the settlement aggregation process is purely CPU, RAM, and local I/O bound. They contend that reaching a volume of pending settlements large enough to materially slow down block production on a block-to-block basis is practically infeasible under realistic operating conditions. 18

title: External RPC dependencies in consensus logic allow validators to be stalled
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_request_for_funds.go :188 , the CreateRequestForFunds message handler invokes VerifyRFFSignature , which is implemented in x/chainabstraction/evmapi/evmapi.go:73-88 . That routine interacts with an external RPC that communicates with another blockchain (e.g., Ethereum, FUEL). Any slowdown, outage, or inconsistent response from that RPC endpoint prevents the transaction from completing and risks diverging results across validators. The same dependency appears in x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_double_check_tx.go:38-54 , where MsgDoubleCheckTx passes vote-extension packets into VerifyVEPacket , implemented in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/ve_verifier.go:55-70 . Inside VerifyVEPacket , both HasWitnessedRequest and VerifyFillerAddress functions perform further live external contract calls. Finally, VerifyVoteExtensionHandler in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/abci/vote_extension.go:187-229 reuses VerifyVEPacket when checking vote extensions during consensus. These executions are consensus-critical, they run on every validator, must be deterministic, and block progress while waiting for the external RPC. An attacker who rate-limits or corrupts responses from any of the referenced RPC providers, or an accidental provider outage, can therefore halt the inclusion of the affected messages, cause vote extensions to be rejected, and ultimately stall block production. Recommendation We recommend removing external RPC dependencies from consensus-critical paths. Signature and state checks should either rely solely on locally available data, be reproduced within the chain via pre-verified proofs, or be performed off-chain before submission, so validators no longer depend on live RPC calls during message handling or vote extension verification. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that the decision not to perform local signature verification is intentional and driven by various design considerations. They further state that this concern is partially mitigated through system design and other layers within the architecture. 19

title: Missing minimum block confirmation margin allows external reorgs to invalidate verified requests
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/ve_verifier.go:52-70 , the VerifyVEPacket function calls HasWitnessedRequest for deposit packets and VerifyFillerAddress for fulfilment packets to verify whether the request has been executed on the external destination chain. However, the implementation does not require a minimum block confirmation depth or a finalized milestone on the external chain before marking a request as valid. If a short-lived reorganization occurs on the external chain (for example, on Polygon), the previously observed event may disappear while the chainabstraction module continues treating the request as settled, enabling incorrect fulfillments or releasing funds without a corresponding on-chain event. This exposure allows an adversary to exploit transient forks to satisfy off-chain settlement requirements that the canonical chain never confirms, resulting in a loss of funds for the protocol. Recommendation We recommend requiring a minimum number of block confirmations or a finalized milestone on the external chain. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding, noting that 1-block confirmation was an intentional design choice and that the associated risks were intended to be communicated in the overall system design documentation. However, they concur that while 1-block confirmations may be acceptable on chains like Ethereum Mainnet, chains such as Polygon experience more frequent reorgs, making this assumption unsafe across all supported networks. They further state that this will be addressed in the rearchitected system.

title: Fetching vote extension events without timeouts can stall consensus
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/abci/vote_extension.go:136 , the ExtendVoteHandler function launches a goroutine per external chain that invokes FetchEvents without ever applying a timeout. Inside FetchEvents , calls such as chain.Interface.GetRelevantLogsInBlockRange executes against external RPC providers without a deadline, so a slow or unresponsive endpoint can block the goroutine. Because the handler waits on an errgroup for every goroutine to finish, a single blocked 20 request can prevent the ABCI method from returning its vote extension in time, preventing cross-chain bridge intents from being included in blocks. Recommendation We recommend enforcing a timeout for fetching events from external chains. Status: Resolved

title: Unsupported settlement chain stops CA processing for all settlements
body: In the handleNewBlockActual function in ca-node:vservice/settlement_ev.go:60 , the code returns an error when a settlement references a chain identifier that is not present in the node's local registry. Because the Cosmos-side accepts arbitrary chain identifiers, and other solvers might support a larger variety of chains, it is possible to have settlements for chains that a given solver does not support. Once such a settlement is encountered, the function exits early, and the handleNewBlockActual function aborts the entire batch, which leaves every other settlement in the same response unprocessed. The offending settlement remains in the on-chain list, so subsequent blocks will continue to trigger the same failure, effectively halting settlement processing for that solver. Recommendation We recommend replacing the early return with logic that skips unsupported settlements, for example, by continuing the loop after logging the condition so the solver can keep processing the remaining valid settlements. Status: Resolved

title: Disabling libp2p limits enables remote DoS
body: In ca-node:internal/p2p/p2p.go:52 , the CreateNewP2PSetup function instantiates the libp2p resource manager with rcmgr.NewFixedLimiter(rcmgr.InfiniteLimits) , which disables all accounting of streams, memory, and file descriptors. When the limits are infinite, the resource manager cannot enforce per-peer or system-wide caps, so any connected counterparty can spawn unbounded streams or request excessive buffers. 21 Although the connection manager still bounds the number of peers, a single malicious peer can monopolize memory or descriptors until the process exhausts host resources. This enables a remote denial-of-service condition against every node that adopts this configuration. Recommendation We recommend configuring the libp2p resource manager with finite, environment-appropriate limits (for example, by using rcmgr.InfiniteLimits.ToPartialLimitConfig().Build(...) and overriding critical ceilings) so that abusive peers are throttled before they can exhaust local resources. Status: Resolved

title: Transient DSG send failures slip through retries and stall key operations
body: In ca-node:vservice/dsg.go:249-256 , the closure passed to the retry helper returns the outer err variable when a.p2pSend fails, even though that variable remains nil . Because the retry loop interprets a nil return value as success, libp2p transmission failures do not trigger another attempt, and the error never propagates to callers. As a result, in addition to logging the incorrect err variable, any temporary network disruption causes the sending node to drop critical DSG messages, halting distributed key generation and signing across the cluster. Recommendation We recommend returning the actual err2 value from the closure, logging it for visibility, and allowing the retry backoff to execute. Status: Resolved

title: Replayed DSG messages crash CA nodes through closed channel writes
body: In ca-nodevservice/dsg.go:119-163 , the setupDSGStreamHandler function accepts any correctly signed DSG payload and forwards it to MessageKeeper without freshness or nonce checks. Because the handler does not enforce replay protection, an allowlisted malicious participant can resend any previously valid DSG message at will. In vservice/msgkeeper.go:85-96 , the ProcessMsg function closes the round's channel 22 once the expected message count is reached but retains the round entry in MessageKeeper.rounds . Therefore, a replayed payload still passes the check in the HasRound function, and ProcessMsg attempts to enqueue it on the closed channel, which triggers a panic: send on closed channel , causing the service to crash. Recommendation We recommend removing the round from MessageKeeper.rounds immediately after its channel is closed. Status: Resolved

title: Incomplete fee grant implementation
body: In ca-node:vservice/feegrant.go:30-36 , the NewMsgGrantAllowance function creates a fee grant with hardcoded placeholder values that are not production-ready. Specifically, the allowance uses a test denom " test " with an amount of 1 , and sets Expiration to nil, meaning the grant never expires. Additionally, the createFeeGrant entry point is publicly accessible with no access controls or rate limiting. This allows any user, including external users who do not use the protocol, to repeatedly call this endpoint to receive unlimited fee grants and avoid paying transaction fees. Recommendation We recommend implementing the following changes before production deployment: ● Replace the hardcoded " test " denom with the actual denom to be granted for allowance ● Implement a proper expiration timestamp instead of setting Expiration to nil ● Add rate limiting to the createFeeGrant endpoint to prevent spam, for example, consider implementing per-user limits or cooldown periods for fee grant requests Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that the Cosmos chain operates as a feeless network, and the fee-grant mechanism exists solely to initialize the account sequence. They recognize the potential denial-of-service vector and intend to address it through alternative mitigations outside the scope of this particular logic. 23

title: Switching the connected wallet continues to use the previous EVM address
body: In nexus-sdk:packages/core/sdk/ca-base/ca.ts:416 , the createCosmosWallet function retrieves and persists the cached SIWE signature under this._evm.address . That field is only populated by the _setEVMProvider function in lines 293-307 , which is only called once during initialize , while the accountsChanged hook in lines 286-290 merely re-initializes the stack without refreshing this._evm.address . After the provider reports an account change, the SDK continues to index SIWE signatures, Cosmos wallet derivation, and the bridge options with the previous account. As a result, downstream flows such as balance queries, allowance checks, refund scans, and bridge intent execution run against the wrong address, even though the wallet extension now exposes a different account. This creates the risk that value-moving operations or approvals are applied to the wrong account, preventing the newly selected account from interacting reliably. Recommendation We recommend updating this._evm.address whenever the provider's accountsChanged event fires (for example, by reusing the _setEVMProvider function with the current account) and ensuring SIWE signatures, Cosmos wallet derivation, and bridge handlers always reference the freshly selected address. Status: Resolved

title: Compromised SIWE signature enables permanent theft of derived Cosmos and ephemeral wallets
body: In nexus-sdk:packages/core/sdk/ca-base/ca.ts:415-427 , the _createCosmosWallet function derives both the Cosmos signer and the Calibur "ephemeral" EVM account from a SIWE signature obtained once per EVM address. That signature is stored in browser storage, and the SIWE message hardcodes nonce and issuedAt . As a consequence, any script that can read from local storage, including injected XSS, malicious dependencies, or another extension on the same origin, can exfiltrate the cached signature and deterministically reconstruct the same private key pair indefinitely. This yields full control over the delegated EVM wallet, the Cosmos account, existing intents, and any future Calibur batched calls without further user interaction. 24 Recommendation We recommend eliminating the static SIWE seed and avoiding plaintext storage of reusable signing material. A safer pattern is to remove the hardcoded nonce and timestamp, derive the key once, and persist the resulting secret only in encrypted form (e.g., using WebCrypto with a user-provided passphrase or a hardware-backed WebAuthn credential). Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that any party with access to the EIP-1193 provider can prompt the user to re-sign the SIWE message, a routine user interaction, and thereby re-derive the same private key. They further state that guarding against adversaries capable of compromising running code within the JavaScript context, including access to storage, RAM, or the provider itself, is not feasible. Since an app developer could already maliciously abuse users regardless of this design choice, the finding does not introduce additional trust assumptions. Additionally, because SIWE signatures are domain-bound, a compromised derived key does not affect other applications.

title: CreateProtocolFees lacks an authorization check, allowing anyone to set themselves as admin
body: In the CreateProtocolFees function in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_protocol_fees.go:13- 35 , there is no authorization check to verify that the caller is authorized to create protocol fees. The function only checks whether protocol fees already exist in lines 17-20 . If they don't, any user can call this function to set themselves as the protocolFees admin, set arbitrary fee percentages, and configure fee recipients. This allows any attacker to be the first to call CreateProtocolFees after the chain launch, thereby gaining complete control over protocol fees. Recommendation We recommend adding an authorization check similar to UpdateProtocolFees or MsgUpdateParams , such as checking that msg.Creator matches the module authority k.GetAuthority , requiring this to be a governance proposal, or checking against a predefined admin address set during genesis initialization. Status: Resolved 25

title: Signature verification failure enables zero solver addresses and burns settlements
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/evmapi/evmapi.go:90-107 , the VerifyGenericMessageSignature function returns universeabstraction.ZeroCommonAddress together with a nil error whenever crypto.SigToPub fails to recover a public key. The caller function validateSolverDataAddresses in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_solver_data.go:22-61 only checks the error value before comparing the supplied address with the returned signer. Because both values are zero, a solver that accidentally submits the zero address together with an invalid signature is accepted. Downstream, the settlement flow in ExecuteVE in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/ve_exec.go:56-187 records this zero address as the payout recipient, so the protocol schedules settlements to 0x000…0 . Those transfers are unrecoverable, resulting in a direct loss of funds for the solver and breaking settlements for that request. Recommendation We recommend propagating the signature recovery error (or returning a dedicated failure) from VerifyGenericMessageSignature and rejecting zero addresses explicitly in the solver-data validation so that settlement recipients cannot resolve to the zero address. Status: Resolved

title: Using log.Fatal can halt the validator
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/evmapi/evm_logs.go:37 , the GetRelevantLogsInBlockRange function calls log.Fatal when the vault ABI fails to parse, and in lines 68 and 78 , the same function invokes log.Fatal when unpacking the Deposit and Fulfilment logs. Because log.Fatal terminates the process through os.Exit(1) , it forces the Cosmos SDK node to stop rather than returning an error through the module's consensus-safe path. This turns external log data into a validator-wide denial-of-service, requiring operator intervention to restart and leaving the validator unable to participate in consensus while the fault persists. 26 Recommendation We recommend replacing the log.Fatal calls with error returns (or module-level logging) so that parsing failures propagate through the Cosmos SDK error handling path, allowing the validator to report the failure without terminating. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that the ABI data is hardcoded and cannot return an error in practice under normal operation. Consequently, the unhandled error path is considered harmless.

title: Known vulnerable Go dependencies
body: In xarchain:go.mod and ca-node:go.mod , a large set of direct dependencies is pinned, and running govulncheck ./... reports several outstanding advisories for the current dependency graph. Each flagged advisory indicates that the project links against code containing publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, so deploying the current build leaves the binary exposed to those attack surfaces. Recommendation We recommend upgrading any dependencies reported as vulnerable. Status: Resolved

title: Gas refund flag in deposit packet is ignored by the Cosmos chain
body: In ca-node:vservice/rff.go:129-133 , the service constructs MsgDoubleCheckTx packets with a DepositVEPacket payload that sets GasRefunded to true . However, the Cosmos application processes the same packet type using a version that only exposes the Id field, so the gas refund flag is silently discarded when the message is decoded, leading to potential mismatches in expected behavior between the CA service and the chain. Recommendation We recommend updating both the service and the Cosmos module to share an identical protobuf definition for DepositVEPacket . Status: Resolved 27

title: Default price of 1.0 for unknown tokens
body: In ca-node:vservice/unified_bal.go:45-47, when GetPriceForCurrencyFromPOD returns ErrInvalidCurrency because a token's price is not found in the price oracle data, the code defaults the price to 1.0 by setting price = apd.New(1, 0) . This means any token without a registered price is treated as having a real-world value of 1.0 USD. This causes the unified balance report to display inflated and inaccurate values. Users holding large quantities of worthless tokens would see their total balance incorrectly reported as significant USD values, misrepresenting their actual holdings. We classify this issue as minor, as it affects data accuracy and user experience but does not directly compromise protocol security or result in a loss of funds. Recommendation We recommend changing the default behavior when a token price is not found. Instead of defaulting to 1.0 , the code should either return an error to indicate that the balance cannot be accurately calculated or default to 0 to avoid inflating balance reports with worthless tokens. Status: Resolved

title: Signed batched call signatures never expire, enabling replay when leaked
body: In nexus-sdk:packages/core/sdk/ca-base/swap/sbc.ts:24-51 , the createBatchedCallSignature function encodes the deadline field of the SignedBatchedCall payload as maxUint256 . The same hardcoded value is propagated when the serialized request is assembled in lines 73-146 via the createSBCTxFromCalls function. Because these signatures never expire, any signed payload that leaks prior to on-chain submission remains executable indefinitely until its nonce is consumed. An adversary who gains access to such a signature can execute the batched call at any time, even after the user's intent has changed, enabling the unauthorized execution of stale operations and potentially resulting in asset transfers or other unwanted state changes. 28 Recommendation We recommend exposing a short, caller-configurable deadline for batched call signatures. Status: Resolved

title: Params validate performs no validation, allowing invalid parameters to be stored
body: In the Validate function in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/types/params.go:30-32 , the function always returns nil without validating any fields. The Params struct contains sensitive configuration, including Universe enum values, ChainID byte slices, DisabledTokens byte slices, and other nested configs. This allows governance proposals or genesis initialization to set invalid or malformed parameters. Recommendation We recommend implementing comprehensive validation in the Validate function to check that UniverseParams are valid. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that this parameter is only configurable via a governance proposal, making additional validation generally unnecessary. They may consider adding explicit validation in a future update as a defensive measure.

title: Protocol fees messages lack validation for fee configuration fields
body: In the ValidateBasic functions in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/types/messages_protocol_fees.go:11-17 and 21-26 , only the Creator address is validated, while all other fields are accepted without validation. This is problematic because these functions may introduce critical misconfiguration issues if invalid parameters are passed. 29 Recommendation We recommend implementing comprehensive validation including checking that FeeBP does not exceed 10000 (100%), validating that Universe enum values are valid, validating ChainID and TokenAddress byte slices have correct lengths for their respective chains, validating Fee byte slices are properly formatted and represent valid amounts, validating Address byte slices in AdminFeeRecipient have correct lengths, checking for duplicate entries in arrays, and ensuring all required fields are present and non-empty where appropriate. Status: Resolved

title: Service startup might hang due to an infinite peer connection retry loop
body: In the main function in ca-node:vservice/main.go:130-141 , a peer ping loop retries indefinitely with no timeout or cancellation. The code waits for a response from each peer in a.dsgNodeDetails.nodes and retries every 10 seconds if a response is not received. If a peer never responds, the startup blocks indefinitely, resulting in a denial-of-service and preventing the application from starting. Recommendation We recommend adding a timeout mechanism, such as a context with a deadline, a maximum retry count, or a timeout for the entire peer connection phase, to ensure startup completes even if some peers are unavailable. Status: Resolved

title: DSG threshold set to 100%
body: In the main function in ca-node:vservice/main.go:107 , the DSG threshold is hardcoded to equal the total number of participants, requiring all nodes to participate in distributed operations. This means any single node failure or unavailability creates a single point of failure. The system cannot tolerate even a single offline or malicious node, making it vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks and operational failures. 30 Recommendation We recommend making the threshold configurable and setting it to a value that provides Byzantine fault tolerance, such as (n/2 + 1) for n nodes, allowing the system to function with up to (n-1)/2 nodes being unavailable or malicious. Status: Resolved

title: Potentially non-deterministic nonce derivation
body: In the createSBCTxFromCalls function in nexus-sdk:packages/core/sdk/ca-base/swap/sbc.ts:100-110 , the authorization nonce is fetched using getTransactionCount with blockTag: 'pending' without synchronization. If multiple SBC transactions are created concurrently, or within a larger window before the next transaction is confirmed, multiple SBC transactions may attempt to use the same nonce, and the latter will fail. Recommendation We recommend implementing deterministic nonce derivation in the createSBCTxFromCalls function. Status: Resolved

title: Missing disabled vote extension check
body: In xarchain:x/chainabstraction/abci/proposal.go:111 , the PreBlocker function checks whether to process vote extensions from the condition req.Height > ctx.ConsensusParams().Abci.VoteExtensionsEnableHeight . The issue is that it does not also verify that vote extensions are enabled (i.e., by checking that VoteExtensionsEnableHeight is non-zero). According to CometBFT documentation , once vote extensions are enabled, they cannot be disabled. Therefore, in the intended operation of the protocol, where vote extensions are enabled at the beginning, this inconsistency does not pose a material risk. The issue also affects the ProcessProposal function in x/chainabstraction/abci/proposal.go:78 . 31 Recommendation We recommend adding validation to ensure that VoteExtensionsEnableHeight is non-zero before processing vote extensions in the PreBlocker and ProcessProposal functions. Status: Resolved

title: Multiple messages return empty responses
body: In the UpdateParams function in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_update_params.go:22 , the function returns an empty MsgUpdateParamsResponse struct with no fields populated. It is best practice to return response attributes that reflect the actions and state changes performed. The following chain abstraction message handlers also return empty responses: ● DoubleCheckTx in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_double_check_tx .go:57 ● CreateSolverData in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_solver_data.go: 91 ● UpdateSolverData in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_solver_data.go: 122 ● CreateProtocolFees in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_protocol_fees.g o:34 ● UpdateProtocolFees in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_protocol_fees. go:61 ● UpdateParams in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_update_params.go:22 ● RefundReq in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/msg_server_refund_req.go:6 6 Recommendation We recommend adding meaningful response fields to the responses mentioned above that accurately reflect the state changes in their respective messages. 32 Status: Acknowledged

title: Missing validation for RPC URLs and vault contract addresses during initialization
body: In the chain initialization loop in xarchain:x/chainabstraction/keeper/keeper.go:452-465 , the code validates that RPC URLs exist and are non-empty in lines 452-460 and that vault contract addresses exist in lines 461-465 , but it does not validate URL format, connectivity, or contract address format/validity. While malformed RPC URLs will eventually cause panics when ethclient.Dial is called in evmapi.NewEVMAPI in line 41 , and invalid contract addresses may cause failures during contract interactions. These errors occur after the initial validation checks pass. Since these values are set during chain initialization and are unlikely to be incorrect, the risk is low. However, configuration errors may not be detected until runtime operations fail. Recommendation We recommend adding validation during initialization: for RPC URLs, perform a simple connectivity check such as calling eth_chainId for EVM chains; for vault contract addresses, perform a simple contract query to verify the address is valid, and the contract exists. This would provide early detection of configuration issues, though given these are init-time configurations, the benefit may be limited. Status: Acknowledged

title: Hardcoded gas limits may cause inefficiency or failures
body: In the createFeeGrant function in ca-node:vservice/feegrant.go:40 , the gas limit is hardcoded to 3_00_000 when submitting the fee grant transaction. This fixed value may not match the actual gas required for the transaction. In addition, this issue is also present in ca-node:vservice/rff.go:142 . Recommendation We recommend making the gas limits configurable and then having a fallback value. Status: Acknowledged 33

title: Setup function can be used by anyone to take control of the gateway contract
body: In the Solidity contract contracts/src/AxelarGatewayMultisig.sol the setup function can be called multiple times by anyone, allowing an adversary to take over control of the key privileged roles. This is due to the function being externally callable and not protected by any pre-condition other than not being callable on the implementation contract directly. However, since the storage contract is that of the proxy this guard does not prevent unauthorized invocations. This issue also applies to contracts/src/AxelarGatewaySinglesig.sol (out of scope). Recommendation We recommend adding access control to this function. Status: Resolved

title: Non-unique key for identifying voting topics implementations may lead to lost proposals
body: In the Solidity contract contracts/src/AdminMultisigBase.sol function the hash of msg.data is used to identify proposal topics. This value is used as a key to store the topic in the eternal storage contract (key-value store). However, msg.data simply encodes functions and parameters, meaning that repeated proposal of the same operation will result in the key being calculated with the same result. In this case, the previous proposal would be overwritten in storage and lost. msg.data can also be malleable due to different libraries or wallets adding trailing zeros which could lead to key mismatch (see issue Manual storage management in upgradability pattern used is error-prone and may lead to storage key conflicts ). Recommendation We recommend adding a unique parameter to the key used to store the topic. Status: Acknowledged 14 The team states that in their use case proposal overwriting is no not problematic and that all used libraries encode msg.data consistently.

title: Gateway contract address depend on token symbol only and might clash
body: Token contracts and burner contracts are deployed using the create2 opcode, in order to deterministically calculate the addresses on both sides. Since the initialization code remains constant for all tokens the only distinguishing factor for different deployments is the salt used in the address calculation. To this end, the codebase uses the hash of the token symbol. Since the token symbol becomes the only identifier of an asset, tokens with the same symbol will clash, resulting in the same contract address. Effectively, only 3 bytes of input are used to produce a 32-byte hash value. This may lead to accidental overwriting of assets. Recommendation We recommend using values that provide a higher degree of entropy to generate the hash or keeping a registry of asset addresses shared between both sides of the bridge, instead of dynamically calculating the addresses. Status: Acknowledged

title: Expired polls can be voted on
body: In the x/vote/types/types.go module, the Vote method lacks a check whether the poll has been expired, allowing expired polls to be voted on. Recommendation We recommend checking the Expired state. Status: Acknowledged Team Reply: "That is actually desired behaviour. We set the Expired flag after a configured amount of blocks to make it possible to retry a poll (otherwise we could get stuck while voting on deposits, tokens etc) if needed. But an expired poll is not automatically invalid, it just means it hasn't been completed after that configured amount of time. If late voters make the poll succeed after expiry that is not an issue." 15

title: Manual storage management in upgradability pattern used is error-prone and may lead to storage key conflicts
body: The Solidity smart contracts use an eternal storage pattern using a hash of an identifier key as a manual storage pointer.. This introduces a source of potential errors since keys with the same name result in the same hash causing storage to be overwritten. The reverse can also occur if the source of the key calculation may be encoded slightly differently by off-chain libraries. An example of this occurring is the msg.data field used as a key in contracts/src/AdminMultisigBase.sol . This field may have trailing zeros, depending on the wallet implementation used to interact with the smart contract, resulting in different key calculations and failure to look up the correct entry. Recommendation There are a number of alternative patterns for upgradability that provide eternal storage with upgradable logic. In addition, tooling exists automating some of the nuisances of memory management. An example of this is the OpenZeppellin upgradability framework ( https://docs.openzeppelin.com/upgrades-plugins/1.x/ ) Status: Acknowledged

title: ExportGenesis should return the genesis state instead of nil
body: In the x/axelarnet module, the genesis export returns nil . Recommendation We recommend returning the module's genesis state variable in the ExportGenesis method. Status: Resolved

title: Panic used for non-eligible validators in inflation calculation breaks iteration for the other eligible bonded validator
body: 16 Function handleTssInflation in x/reward/abci.go uses panic during the bonded validator iteration when a validator is found to be not eligible. This will skip the other eligible bonded validators. Recommendation We recommend skipping only the uneligible validator and continuing to handle other validators in the bonded validator list. Status: Acknowledged Team Reply: "An error received from GetValidatorIllegibility is a panic-worthy scenario since a bonded validator should have a corresponding consensus address. This follows standard Cosmos practice of calling panic when an error is received from a function that is never expected to fail."

title: Single invalid key causes subsequent valid keys to be skipped when batch-registering external keys
body: In the RegisterExternalKeys function in x/tss/keeper/msg_server.go , the iteration skips valid keys when an invalid key is present in the slice by returning from the method when it finds any validation error. Recommendation We recommend validating all the keys first and then only calling adding valid keys. Alternatively, the method may choose to panic and register no key at all. Status: Acknowledged Team Reply: "This is not applicable since returning an error reverts to the original state in Cosmos, same as calling a panic, so none of the external keys will be set if one is invalid. To reply to Point 10, we expect a precise number of keys so we can't ignore invalid keys, and we think it's bad practice to process a message with any invalid input (this should never occur anyways from an honest user)."

title: RouteIBCTransfer is not considering all the valid chain entries in case of error during iteration
body: 17 In the x/axelarnet module message server function, the RouteIBCTransfers returns on encountering an error during iterations. This will cause the method to skip all other entries in the slice over which the iteration is performed. Recommendation We recommend using continue instead of return . Status: Resolved

title: Extreme value check is performed on inflation
body: In the validateExternalChainVotingInflationRate and validateTssRelativeInflationRate functions of x/reward/types/params.go validation performed on the parameter for inflations are done at the extreme edge case of values 0 and 1. However, when the value is set to 0, it will cause the reward to be calculated as 0, which is not in favour of accounts or validators who are actively participating in the protocol activity, therefore discouraging participation. On the other extreme, a value of 1 might provide very large rewards, which also negatively affect the protocols economics. Recommendation We recommend incorporating min and max values and relevant validation for the inflation parameters to exclude extreme values. Status: Acknowledged Team Reply: " TssRelativeInflationRate specifies the percentage of the Tendermint inflation rate that is added as a bonus, and thus is naturally capped by the current Tendermint inflation rate. In fact, we planned to set this to 100%, i.e 1.0 for the mainnet. And initially, we do want the ability to disable inflation rewards, i.e set it to

title: In general, long term this should be governable by the community, and so we haven't added many restrictions." 11. Lack of retrial limit for IBC transfers might cause validator funds to drain
body: In audit-axelar-core/x/axelarnet/module.go , IBC message error handling is handled. 18 In case of negative acknowledgement or timeout, the code resolves to retry the same packet again and again without maintaining any maximum retrial counter. Every time a relayer is relaying a packet to the destination chain, it has to pay transaction fees. The continuous resending attempts might, therefore, lead to significant funds drainage in the form of transaction fees. Recommendation We recommend implementing a maximum limit for retries. Status: Acknowledged Team Reply: "On packet-timeout, it's guaranteed by IBC that it won't timeout again. We don't think the acknowledgement error case is concerning unless there is a bug in the IBC protocol itself with the refund logic. And we don't want to miss any packets for our protocol."

title: Access control modified with major side-effects introduces logic in eternal storage
body: In contracts/src/AdminMultisigBase.sol the onlyAdmin modifier is used to ensure only an admin role can call certain methods. However, the modifier also modifies state and introduces a significant amount of logic. This introduces two problems: Firstly, it breaks with common conventions of access control modifier naming and introduces side-effects, including aborting in executing without reverting in some cases. Secondly, the use of this modifier introduces significant logic into the eternal storage part of the contracts, breaking the upgradability paradigm used. Recommendation We recommend not implementing any state-changing logic in access control modifiers. Status: Acknowledged

title: Excessive gas usage through burner contracts
body: On the Ethereum side assets are burnt by deploying a special-purpose burner contract that self-destructs. There seems to be no advantage to using this approach and the gas usage is much higher than commonly used ERC-20 extensions for burning tokens. 19 Recommendation We recommend using a permissioned burn method as part of the ERC-20 implementation. Status: Resolved

title: Solidity version pragma allows for versions with security vulnerabilities
body: The codebase allows any Solidity compiler version from 0.8 to less than 0.9. A number of important compiler bugs have recently been fixed. In particular, version 0.8.4 fixed important security issues. Recommendation Consider locking the version pragma to a specific compiler version, preferably 0.8.4 or above. Status: Acknowledged 20

title: Missing TLS credentials and HMAC key in gRPC client enables credential compromise and MITM attacks
body: In finality-provider:eotsmanager/cmd/eotsd/daemon/unlock.go:36-71 , the unlockKeyring function initializes a gRPC client connection using the eotsclient.NewEOTSManagerGRpcClient method while explicitly passing an empty string as the HMAC key. This disables HMAC-based client authentication. Although the function ProcessHMACKey emits a warning, it permits the connection to proceed without enforcing any authentication. Furthermore, the gRPC connection is configured with insecure.NewCredentials , resulting in unencrypted and unauthenticated communication. Consequently, the Unlock method transmits sensitive data, including the EOTS public key and user passphrase, without confidentiality or integrity protections. This introduces the risk of credential compromise or man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. Recommendation We recommend enforcing strict authentication and secure transport in gRPC connections by: ● Replacing insecure.NewCredentials with credentials configured with proper TLS certificates. ● Ensuring a valid and securely stored HMAC key is passed to NewEOTSManagerGRpcClient , thereby enabling the HMACUnaryClientInterceptor . Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #487 .

title: Retrieving staking transactions using incorrect page increments results in skipped transactions
body: In vigilante:btcstaking-tracker/stakingeventwatcher/stakingeventwatch er.go:995 , the fetchStakingTxsByEvent function retrieves staking transaction hashes 14 via the paginated query function StakingTxHashesByEvent , providing i and batchSize as the page and page-entry-limit parameters, respectively. However, after each call, i is incorrectly increased by batchSize instead of being incremented by 1 . If more than batchSize staking transactions exist between startHeight and endHeight , up to batchSize pages of transactions are skipped. As a result, the watcher silently omits delegations and never revisits those heights. Recommendation We recommend incrementing i by 1 after each fetch operation. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #359 .

title: Missing message size enforcement in DeliverTx enables oversized IBC messages payload injection
body: In babylon:app/ante/ibc_msg_size.go:25-44 , the AnteHandle function of the IBCMsgSizeDecorator validates IBC message size constraints only during the CheckTx phase. This validation includes limits on message, memo, and address sizes for MsgTransfer and MsgSendTx messages. However, no equivalent enforcement occurs during the DeliverTx phase, which is responsible for block execution. As a result, malicious proposers can bypass mempool checks and inject oversized IBC or ICA messages directly into blocks without the risk of being slashed. This forces other validators to process potentially resource-exhausting payloads, introducing a denial of service vector within the consensus mechanism. Recommendation We recommend extending size validations to the DeliverTx phase. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1081 . 15

title: Unbounded growth in historical finality provider rewards leads to state bloat
body: The IncrementFinalityProviderPeriod function in babylon:x/incentive/keeper/reward_tracker.go:214-256 persistently stores historical reward records in the finalityProviderHistoricalRewards map. The stored data, represented by newFpHistoricalRwd , includes cumulative reward values that grow monotonically due to repeated additions of current reward per satoshi. This storage pattern is triggered by common operations such as delegation updates, staking changes, and reward withdrawals However, no mechanism exists to remove old records that are no longer needed to process rewards withdrawal or delegation modifications. As a result, the blockchain state could expand unboundedly and increase storage costs and requirements for validators. Recommendation We recommend implementing a pruning strategy that retains only necessary historical data used in current reward calculations. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding without a need for immediate resolution as it involves an optimization in storage. The inefficiency is not directly exploitable. The client plans to address it in an upcoming release and has created #812 to track this.

title: Insufficient validation of genesis' RefundableMsgHashes allows malformed entries
body: The validateMsgHashes function in babylon:x/incentive/types/genesis.go:226-238 verifies that each hash in the RefundableMsgHashes list is non-empty and unique. However, it lacks enforcement of structural or length constraints on the hash values. This permits malformed or arbitrarily long strings to be included in the genesis file. 16 Recommendation We recommend strengthening the validation logic by enforcing at least a maximum allowed length for each hash. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1066 .

title: Unsynchronized EOTS private key retrieval causes potential panic and memory corruption
body: In the getKeyFromMap function in finality-provider:eotsmanager/localmanager.go:402-414 , the code accesses the privateKeys map without holding the required mutex lock. The function assumes callers always hold the LocalEOTSManager.mm mutex, but the callstack SignSchnorrSigFromKeyname , eotsPrivKeyFromKeyName , getKeyFromMap violates this assumption. Concurrent access to Go maps triggers runtime panics, creating a denial-of-service vector for the eotsd daemon, and in Go runtime bug scenarios, could cause memory corruption, leading to private key exposure. We classify this as Minor because currently the SignSchnorrSigFromKeyname function is only called from a CLI command handler, and the risk of concurrent access is negligible. It requires immediate attention, however, as an unaware future maintainer may use the function in a concurrent context. Recommendation We recommend acquiring the LocalEOTSManager.mm mutex within getKeyFromMap or document and enforcing the locking requirement in all calling functions to prevent concurrent map access. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #480 . 17

title: Passphrase handling in command line arguments
body: In the unlockKeyring function, defined in finality-provider:eotsmanager/cmd/eotsd/daemon/unlock.go:36 , the passphrase is passed as a command-line argument. However, this could expose the passphrase in shell history. While the daemon is likely used in controlled environments, it is best practice to avoid passing sensitive information via command-line arguments. Recommendation We recommend using environment variables or secure input methods for passphrase handling. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #487 .

title: Incomplete BLS key validation
body: In babylon:x/checkpointing/types/bls_key.go:29 , the ValidatorWithBlsKeySet.Validate function checks if the BLS key can be unmarshaled, but does not verify if it is a valid point on the BLS12-381 curve. This could potentially allow invalid public keys to be accepted and unexpected errors or results when those keys are used. Recommendation We recommend adding explicit validation of the BLS public key point. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1129 .

title: Usage of deprecated x/crisis module allows attackers to DoS the chain
body: The Babylon Genesis chain currently employs the x/crisis module to allow any participant to halt the chain in the event of an invariant violation by sending a MsgVerifyInvariant 18 message. This mechanism is intended to increase the robustness of the network by enabling the detection of critical inconsistencies. However, the module is deprecated as indicated in GHSA-qfc5-6r3j-jj22 and GHSA-w5w5-2882-47pc because it fails to induce a panic within transaction processing, thus treating broken invariants as reverted transactions. Additionally, as reported in the CVEs, processing MsgVerifyInvariant messages incurs significant computational overhead, while the fee does not align with the computational demand, making these transactions cheaper relative to their processing cost. Recommendation We recommend removing the x/crisis module. Instead, simulation tests should be enhanced, and the implementation of the x/circuit module could be evaluated. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1156 .

title: Plaintext password storage for BLS key decryption undermines key confidentiality
body: In babylon:cmd/babylond/cmd/verify_val_bls_key.go:20 , the VerifyValidatorBlsKey command accepts a --bls-password-file flag, allowing users to supply a password for decrypting the BLS key from a file. However, this file is expected to store the password in plaintext, negating the security benefits of key encryption. Any attacker with access to the local filesystem can trivially read the password and decrypt the associated BLS key. This creates a false sense of security while effectively negating encrypted key storage with plaintext password exposure and introducing significant risks in validator setups. Recommendation We recommend eliminating reliance on plaintext password files. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding with the note that plaintext storage is only one of the options for specifying the BLS password, with more secure options available. The client plans to deprecate plaintext file support and help users migrate in future releases. Issue to track for the resolution: #1165 19

title: Unbounded state growth due to unpruned BTC staking gauges
body: The RewardBTCStaking function in babylon:x/incentive/keeper/btc_staking_gauge.go:19 maintains a new BTC staking gauge for each height but never removes old gauges after they are used. However, this leads to unbounded state growth as the chain progresses, since each height's gauge data remains in the state store indefinitely. Recommendation We recommend pruning the staking gauges after they are used. However, the removal of previous gauges may impact the QueryBTCStakingGaugeRequest query, so it may also be required to update the query to note that it will not return inactive gauges. Status: Acknowledged The client acknowledges this finding as an optimization involving the pruning of historical states without a direct exploitability. The client plans to address it in upcoming releases. Issue to track for the resolution: #812 .

title: Missing length validation of TransactionKey.Hash in the x/btccheckpointing module
body: In babylon:x/btccheckpoint/types/types.go:207-212 , the TransactionKey.Validate method verifies that the Hash field is not nil . However, it does not verify the length of the Hash , which should match the expected size of the Bitcoin block hash. This omission potentially leads to state corruption if an invalid genesis file is used. Recommendation We recommend validating that the length of the Hash field matches the expected size of a Bitcoin block hash within the Validate method. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1099 . 20

title: Incomplete validation of RawCheckpointWithMeta permits inconsistent genesis configuration
body: In babylon:x/checkpointing/types/checkpoint.go:5-19 , the Validate method validates the Ckpt and BlsMultiSig fields. However, validation for other fields like Status and BlsAggrPk is missing. This allows the genesis configuration to bypass constraints enforced during runtime operations, potentially leading to inconsistencies. Consequently, an improperly configured genesis file could result in a checkpoint with an invalid state, such as a sealed checkpoint without a valid BLS aggregation public key. Additionally, the call to BlsMultiSig.ValidateBasic is made twice if the field is not nil , first when calling Ckpt.ValidateBasic and then again straight afterwards. Recommendation We recommend expanding the Validate method to encompass all fields within RawCheckpointWithMeta , ensuring all invariants are enforced during genesis initialization. Additionally, we recommend removing the second call to BlsMultiSig.ValidateBasic . Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1120 .

title: Unvalidated genesis state in x/mint module leads to chain halt risks
body: In babylon:x/mint/keeper/genesis.go:9-14 , the InitGenesis function does not validate the Minter field of the GenesisState before committing it to storage. If the Minter configuration is invalid, it may lead to zero rewards being produced per block. This would break the invariant in the x/incentive module's RewardBTCStaking function, called within the x/finality module EndBlocker , which will panic and halt the chain if there is no reward gauge set for height being processed. A reward gauge is only set if a non-zero amount of minted rewards is intercepted by the HandleCoinsInFeeCollector function in babylon:x/incentive/keeper/intercept_fee_collector.go:13-35 . 21 Recommendation We recommend calling the GenesisState.Validate method during the InitGenesis function to ensure the Minter is properly configured, as well as validating other genesis state fields. Additionally, to defend against chain halts, set an empty rewards gauge in the HandleCoinsInFeeCollector in the event of zero rewards being intercepted. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1018 .

title: The x/btcstaking module GenesisState lacks complete validation
body: In babylon:x/btcstaking/types/genesis.go:24-53 , the GenesisState.Validate function checks the Params , LargestBtcReorg and AllowedStakingTxHashes fields. However, it lacks validation for the FinalityProviders , BtcDelegations , BlockHeightChains , BtcDelegators , and Events fields. This allows a genesis state to be committed that may be inconsistent with the application logic, potentially leading to unexpected behavior. Recommendation We recommend validating all GenesisState fields where it is possible to do so. Status: Resolved The client fixed the issue in #1123 .

title: Incorrect active finality provider validation in the x/finality module GenesisState
