title: Unvalidated auction_end_time allows silently closing or reopening deposits
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:226-228 and in instantiation in line 29 , auction_end_time is accepted without any validation. Setting it to a past timestamp immediately closes the deposit window. More notably, because UpdateConfig is only gated on last_address.is_none() && !is_finished , the owner can reset a past end time to a future value in the window between the deposit period ending and the first settlement batch running, effectively reopening deposits. Original depositors would have their shares silently diluted by the new deposits. Recommendation We recommend validating that auction_end_time is strictly in the future at both instantiation and in UpdateConfig , and preventing it from being changed once the original end time has elapsed. Status: Resolved

title: Owner can reduce total_usdc_budget to zero after users have committed funds they cannot withdraw
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:235-237 , the UpdateConfig function allows the owner to set total_usdc_budget to any value, including zero, as long as no settlement batch has started. Since there is no withdrawal mechanism in the contract, users who have already deposited claim_token_denom cannot retrieve their tokens. If the owner reduces total_usdc_budget to zero before settlement, the pro-rata share formula yields zero for every depositor, no CLAIMS entries are written, and all deposited tokens are burned at the end of settlement. Users permanently lose their deposited tokens and receive nothing in return. We classify this issue as minor since the UpdateConfig function can only be called by the owner. 11 Recommendation We recommend only allowing total_usdc_budget to be increased, never decreased, at least once the first deposit has been made, given that users are committing funds with an expectation of the announced budget. Status: Resolved

title: Burning an IBC voucher does not burn the underlying tokens in escrow on the source chain
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:185-190 , the final settlement batch emits a BankMsg::Burn for the full total_deposited amount of claim_token_denom . If claim_token_denom is an IBC-bridged token, burning the voucher does not trigger a burn of the original tokens on the source chain: it only destroys the local representation. The tokens that were escrowed on the source chain when the IBC transfer was originally made remain permanently locked there. We classify this issue as minor since the claim_token_denom value can only be set by the owner at instantiation or in the UpdateConfig function. Recommendation We recommend restricting claim_token_denom to tokenfactory or native denoms only, rejecting IBC denoms at instantiation and in UpdateConfig . Status: Acknowledged

title: Changing claim_token_denom after deposits corrupts accounting and permanently bricks settlement
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:229-231 , the UpdateConfig function allows the owner to change claim_token_denom at any point before the first settlement batch, even after users have already deposited under the original denom. This creates several compounding issues. First, the TOTAL_DEPOSITED counter and all DEPOSITS map entries remain unchanged after the denom change. They reflect amounts of the original token. Users can deposit the new token and their amounts are added to TOTAL_DEPOSITED as if they are the same unit 12 as the original token. The share computation during settlement then mixes amounts of two different tokens in the pro-rata formula, producing economically meaningless results. Second, and more critically, the final settlement batch emits BankMsg::Burn { denom: claim_token_denom, amount: total_deposited } where total_deposited includes the sum of both old and new token amounts, but the contract only holds the new token in the amount deposited under the new denom. The burn attempts to burn more of the new token than the contract holds, which would fail. Settlement can never complete, is_finished is never set to true , and all CLAIMS entries written in earlier batches are permanently unclaimable. Original depositors also cannot retrieve their tokens since there is no withdrawal path. We classify this issue as minor since the UpdateConfig function can only be called by the owner. Recommendation We recommend preventing claim_token_denom from being changed once the first deposit has been made. This can be enforced by checking that TOTAL_DEPOSITED is zero before allowing the denom field to be updated in UpdateConfig . Status: Resolved

title: Leftover USDC due to rounding will be irrecoverable
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:159-168 , the execute_settle function computes the user's share portion from the USDC budget based on their deposited amount. The formula used is deposit * total_usdc_budget / total_deposited . Over time, rounding issues may leave some USDC in the contract, which will not be distributed to users. Recommendation We recommend implementing a sweep function that the owner can call after all claims are processed, and sending the remaining USDC to dao_treasury . The dao_treasury is mentioned in README.md:55 , but it was never implemented in the contract, as noted in this finding . Status: Resolved 13

title: README instantiation example contains incorrect and missing fields
body: In README.md:51-57 , the example JSON for instantiation shows fields that do not correspond to the actual InstantiateMsg struct. The example includes auction_duration_seconds and dao_treasury , which do not exist in the struct, and omits the required owner and auction_end_time fields. The actual struct is defined in contracts/auction/src/msg.rs:5-11 . This inconsistency may confuse integrators attempting to instantiate the contract from the documentation. Recommendation We recommend updating the README example to reflect the actual InstantiateMsg fields. Status: Resolved

title: README misleads users about when claiming becomes available
body: In README.md:93 , the claim section states that users can claim their USDC share "after their deposit has been processed in settlement." This implies that a user may claim as soon as their individual deposit is settled in a batch. In reality, execute_claim requires progress.is_finished == true , meaning the entire settlement must complete across all batches before any user can claim. A user whose deposit was processed in the first batch still cannot claim until the final batch finishes. Recommendation : We recommend updating the README to clarify that claiming is only possible after the full settlement process is complete, not after an individual batch processes a given depositor. Status: Resolved 14

title: Direct ownership transfer allows accidental loss of contract control
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:223-225 , the UpdateConfig function allows the owner to transfer ownership to a new address in a single step by passing a new value in the owner field. While this is common practice, it presents a risk for the ownership of the contract to become lost if the owner transfers ownership to an incorrect address. A two-step ownership transfer will allow the current owner to propose a new owner, and then the account that is proposed as the new owner may call a function that will allow them to claim ownership and actually execute the config update. Recommendation We recommend implementing a two-step ownership transfer. The flow can be as follows:

title: The current owner proposes a new owner address that is validated and lowercased. 2. The new owner account claims ownership, which applies the configuration changes. Status: Acknowledged 10. instantiate and update_config emit insufficient event attributes
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:49-51 , the instantiate entry point only emits action and auction_end_time as response attributes. Important configuration parameters such as owner , claim_token_denom , usdc_denom , and total_usdc_budget are not emitted, making it harder to verify the initial contract configuration from transaction history alone. Furthermore, in contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:241 , the UpdateConfig handler returns a response with only the action=update_config attribute. None of the updated field values are emitted. This makes it impossible to determine what changed in a given configuration update from transaction history. Recommendation We recommend emitting all relevant configuration fields as attributes in the instantiate and update_config responses. Status: Resolved 15

title: Non- claim_token_denom funds attached to Deposit are silently locked forever
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:90-95 , execute_deposit iterates info.funds to find the coin matching claim_token_denom and silently ignores all other coins. Any other tokens attached to the same transaction are not returned to the user, so they will be stuck in the contract forever. While blockchains generally do not protect users from sending funds to wrong accounts, reverting extra funds increases the user experience. Recommendation We recommend checking that the transaction contains only the expected Coin and no additional native tokens using https://docs.rs/cw-utils/latest/cw_utils/fn.must_pay.html . Status: Resolved

title: Deposit accumulation uses unchecked addition
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:102 , the global deposit counter is incremented with the += operator: total_deposited += deposit_amount . Using checked_add makes the potential overflow behavior explicit and returns a typed error that can be handled gracefully. Recommendation We recommend replacing total_deposited += deposit_amount with total_deposited = total_deposited.checked_add(deposit_amount)? to make overflow handling explicit and consistent with the rest of the codebase. Status: Resolved 16

title: InsufficientFunds error variant is defined but never used
body: In contracts/auction/src/error.rs:30-31 , the InsufficientFunds variant is declared in the ContractError enum but is never constructed or returned anywhere in the contract. Dead error variants add noise to the error type and may mislead integrators into expecting conditions that are never enforced. Recommendation We recommend removing the InsufficientFunds variant, or implementing the corresponding balance check. Status: Resolved

title: Contract name in cw2 metadata does not match the crate name
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:17 , CONTRACT_NAME is hardcoded as "crates.io:claimer" , while the actual crate is named "auction" . The cw2 standard stores this string on-chain via set_contract_version and is used by migration tooling to verify that a migration target is the correct contract. If a migrate entry point is added in the future and a migration guard checks the stored contract name, it will fail unless the mismatch is accounted for. Recommendation We recommend updating CONTRACT_NAME to "crates.io:auction" to match the actual crate name. Status: Resolved 17

title: Zero-share depositors have their tokens burned with no USDC received and no notification
body: In contracts/auction/src/contract.rs:166-168 , during settlement, a CLAIMS entry is only written when user_share > 0 . Users whose deposit is so small that floor(deposit * total_usdc_budget / total_deposited) == 0 receive no entry and no event is emitted, yet their claim_token_denom tokens are included in the BankMsg::Burn at the end of settlement. Recommendation We recommend emitting an event for zero-share depositors during settlement to maintain an on-chain record that their deposit was processed. Status: Resolved 18

title: tick_undelegation_amount accepts zero, causing undelegation messages with a zero coin amount
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:27-35 and 205-207 , neither instantiate nor execute_update_config validates that tick_undelegation_amount is greater than zero. When tick_undelegation_amount is zero, the execute_tick loop in line 164 computes amount.min(0) for each delegation, producing a StakingMsg::Undelegate with a zero coin amount. The Cosmos SDK rejects zero-amount undelegations, causing every subsequent Tick call to fail for as long as the value remains zero. Recommendation We recommend adding a validation check that tick_undelegation_amount is strictly greater than zero in both instantiate and execute_update_config , returning an error otherwise. More generally, we recommend defining explicit lower and upper bounds for all numeric configuration parameters. Status: Resolved

title: tick_period_seconds can be set too low, risking unbonding entry exhaustion and denial of undelegation
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:27-35 and 208-210 , tick_period_seconds is accepted without any lower bound. On Neutron, the staking module enforces a maximum of 7 concurrent unbonding entries per (delegator, validator) pair within the 20-day unbonding period. If tick_period_seconds is set below approximately 3 days (20 days / 7 entries), the contract may exhaust the unbonding entry limit before existing entries mature. Once the limit is reached, any further Tick call that tries to undelegate from a validator with 7 active entries will fail, and the contract will be unable to process undelegations for those validators until entries mature. 10 Recommendation We recommend enforcing a lower bound on tick_period_seconds of at least unbonding_period / max_entries (approximately 246,000 seconds, for current Neutron parameters) in both instantiate and execute_update_config . Status: Acknowledged

title: tick_undelegation_amount is applied per validator, contradicting its README description as a total cap
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:164 , the undelegation amount per validator is capped with amount.min(config.tick_undelegation_amount) . With N validators, the total amount undelegated in a single tick can reach up to N × tick_undelegation_amount . However, README.md:9 describes this parameter as "Maximum amount of untrn to undelegate in a single tick from all delegated validators," implying a global cap across all validators combined. This discrepancy may cause operators to underestimate the actual undelegation rate when configuring the contract. Recommendation We recommend either updating the README to clarify that tick_undelegation_amount is a per-validator limit, or adjusting the implementation to enforce a global cap across all validators in a single tick. Status: Resolved

title: Overly permissive message dispatch enabling privilege escalation via arbitrary CosmosMsg execution
body: In contracts/auth-proxy/src/contract.rs:34-48 , the execute_forward function implements an over-privileged dispatcher pattern by allowing the contract owner to forward arbitrary CosmosMsg messages without restriction. While access control ensures only the owner can invoke this function, the absence of message-type validation violates the principle of least privilege. 11 If the owner account is compromised, or if downstream contract assumptions evolve, a malicious actor could exploit this functionality to execute unintended operations such as arbitrary contract calls, token transfers, IBC interactions, or other chain-supported message types. This significantly increases the attack surface, potentially enabling unauthorized state transitions, fund movement, or cross-contract interactions. Given that the intended use case only requires StakingMsg::Undelegate and BankMsg::Burn , accepting all CosmosMsg variants introduces unnecessary systemic risk and weakens the security model. Recommendation We recommend enforcing strict input validation by explicitly whitelisting permitted message types (e.g., StakingMsg::Undelegate and BankMsg::Burn ) and rejecting all other variants. Status: Acknowledged

title: Multiple entry points emit insufficient event attributes
body: Multiple entry points emit insufficient event attributes: ● In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:38 , the instantiate entry point only emits action as a response attribute, omitting owner , delegator_contract , tick_undelegation_amount , and tick_period_seconds . ● In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:180-183 , the execute_tick response emits total_delegated but not the total amount actually undelegated in the current tick. ● In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:213 , the UpdateConfig handler returns only action=update_config , without any of the updated field values. This makes it harder to verify or audit the contract state from transaction history alone. Recommendation We recommend emitting all relevant configuration fields as attributes in the instantiate response, accumulating and emitting the total undelegated amount in the execute_tick response, and emitting the new values of all updated fields in execute_update_config . Status: Resolved 12

title: Direct ownership transfer in auth-proxy and undelegations-manager allows accidental loss of contract control
body: In contracts/auth-proxy/src/contract.rs:50-65 , the execute_update_owner handler immediately replaces the stored owner with the new address provided by the caller. Similarly, in contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:199-201 , execute_update_config replaces the owner field in a single step. While this is common practice, it presents a risk for the ownership of the contract to become lost if the owner transfers ownership to an incorrect address. A two-step ownership transfer will allow the current owner to propose a new owner, and then the account that is proposed as the new owner may call a function that will allow them to claim ownership and actually execute the config update. Recommendation We recommend implementing a two-step ownership transfer. The flow can be as follows: ● The current owner proposes a new owner address that is validated and lowercased. ● The new owner account claims ownership, which applies the configuration changes. Status: Acknowledged

title: Error variants in ContractError are unused
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/error.rs:12-29 , the ContractError enum declares six variants ( DepositPeriodEnded , DepositPeriodNotEnded , ZeroDeposit , AuctionSettled , NoClaimableAmount , and InsufficientFunds ) that are never constructed or returned anywhere in the contract. These appear to be remnants of a previous design. Dead variants add noise to the error type and may mislead integrators into expecting conditions that are never actually enforced. Recommendation We recommend removing all unused error variants from ContractError . Status: Resolved 13

title: Tick and Burn messages can be called by any address
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:74 and 112 , neither execute_burn nor execute_tick restricts the caller. Any address can invoke either message at any time (subject to the tick cooldown in the case of Tick ). The absence of access control means that any external actor can trigger undelegation or burn operations. Recommendation If permissionless execution is intentional for both messages, we recommend documenting this design decision explicitly. Otherwise, we recommend restricting each message to authorized callers, for example, limiting Tick to the cron address and Burn to the owner or the undelegations-manager contract itself. Status: Resolved

title: Incomplete pagination handling leads to delegation starvation and state inconsistency
body: In contracts/undelegations-manager/src/contract.rs:112-131 , the execute_tick function performs a delegation query using a hardcoded pagination limit ( limit: 100) without iterating over additional pages. This results in incomplete processing when the number of delegations exceeds the specified limit. A malicious actor or unfavorable validator ordering could exploit this limitation to ensure certain delegations are consistently excluded from processing, leading to starvation. Recommendation We recommend implementing a batching mechanism with explicit continuation state stored on-chain to guarantee fair processing across multiple ticks. Status: Acknowledged 14

title: Misconfigured governance module permissions causing consensus-halting panic on deposit burn
body: In app/app.go:291-311 , the maccPerms map registers govtypes.ModuleName without the authtypes.Burner permission, resulting in a misconfigured governance module account lacking burn capabilities. Despite this, the governance logic (based on Cosmos SDK v0.53.4) invokes deposit burning via DeleteAndBurnDeposits , which internally calls bankKeeper.BurnCoins . The BurnCoins implementation enforces permission checks and will trigger a panic if the calling module account does not have the Burner role. Given that governance parameters (e.g., BurnVoteVeto = true ) enable deposit burning under certain proposal outcomes (such as vetoed or canceled proposals), this creates a panic condition during the x/gov EndBlocker execution. A malicious actor can exploit this by submitting a proposal that triggers deposit burning (e.g., a vetoed proposal), causing all nodes to panic consistently and halting block production. The panic will occur on all nodes, effectively leading to a persistent chain halt until manual intervention. Recommendation We recommend aligning the governance module account permissions with the upstream Cosmos SDK by granting authtypes.Burner to govtypes.ModuleName in the maccPerms configuration. Status: Resolved

title: Any CosmWasm contract can add cron schedules, bypassing authorization
body: In wasmbinding/message_plugin.go:811-815 , the addSchedule handler has had its authorization check replaced with if false , a dead branch that never executes. The handler then constructs a MsgAddSchedule using the governance module address as the hardcoded Authority field, which satisfies the cron keeper's authority check. As a result, any CosmWasm contract can register arbitrary cron schedules that will execute at every block without any restriction on the caller. 13 An attacker-controlled contract can exploit this to spam cron schedules executing arbitrary messages at block begin or end, potentially griefing the chain, or causing unintended state changes. Recommendation We recommend replacing the dead if false branch with a real authorization check, for example verifying that contractAddr is on a governance-approved allowlist. Note that removeSchedule in wasmbinding/message_plugin.go:860 still restricts the caller to params.Params.SecurityAddress , meaning any contract can add a schedule but only the security DAO can remove one. The authorization model should be consistent across both entry points. Status: Resolved

title: ValidatorDstAddress may equal ValidatorSrcAddress in redelegation messages, causing upgrade failure
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:542-544 , calcRedelegations constructs MsgBeginRedelegate messages using delegation.ValidatorAddress as ValidatorSrcAddress and redelegations[newValIdx].ValidatorAddress as ValidatorDstAddress . If any validator in NewValidatorSet also appears in the current delegation set, the generated message may have an identical source and destination address. The Cosmos SDK rejects self-redelegations, and the resulting error would abort the upgrade handler. Recommendation We recommend adding a check in calcRedelegations to skip generating a redelegation message when ValidatorSrcAddress == ValidatorDstAddress . Status: Resolved

title: calcRedelegations uses delegation shares as token amounts, producing incorrect results when validators have been slashed
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:516-518 , totalDelegatedAmount is computed by summing delegation.Shares across all delegations. In 14 app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:544 , the resulting take value is passed directly as the coin amount in MsgBeginRedelegate via take.TruncateInt() . However, MsgBeginRedelegate.Amount expects a token amount, not a share count. After a slash, a validator's exchange rate deviates from 1:1 (e.g., after a 50% slash, 100 shares are worth 50 tokens), so using shares as token amounts would produce incorrect redelegation sizes. Recommendation We recommend converting shares to token amounts using validator.TokensFromShares(delegation.Shares).TruncateInt() before summing and before constructing MsgBeginRedelegate . Status: Resolved

title: nil DistributionKeeper passed to the wasm keeper prevents distribution messages in CosmWasm contracts
body: In app/app.go:783 , the CosmWasm keeper is initialized with nil for the distrKeeper parameter, with a comment stating that the DistributionKeeper interface is not compatible with the wasm keeper. Any CosmWasm contract that attempts to use distribution messages (e.g., withdraw staking rewards or set a withdrawal address) will panic or fail at runtime. The comment should be re-evaluated now that the native distribution module has been integrated, as the interface mismatch may have been resolved. Recommendation We recommend verifying whether the interface mismatch is still present. Other Cosmos chains have resolved this by passing distributionkeeper.NewQuerier(app.DistributionKeeper) rather than the keeper directly, which may satisfy the expected interface, though this should be confirmed before adoption. If a compatible adapter exists, we recommend passing it instead of nil and removing the stale comment. Status: Resolved 15

title: Incorrect BeginBlocker ordering leading to inconsistent reward accounting
body: In app/app.go:928-935 , the BeginBlocker execution order invokes the slashing module before the mint and distribution modules, violating the expected execution sequence defined in the Cosmos SDK (mint -> distribution -> slashing -> staking). This ordering contradicts both the documented assumption in the codebase and the canonical SDK design, where rewards are first minted and distributed before any slashing logic is applied. By executing slashes prematurely, slash events and validator period updates occur before reward allocation, breaking the distribution module's assumption that slashes are applied after rewards are calculated. This misordering can lead to inconsistencies in the period-based reward accounting model, potentially resulting in incorrect reward distribution to delegators. Additionally, it may violate invariants such as CanWithdrawInvariant, which rely on the correct sequencing of reward allocation and slashing. Recommendation We recommend reordering the BeginBlocker execution to align with the Cosmos SDK standard sequence: ensure that the mint and distribution modules execute before the slashing module. Status: Resolved

title: Identical minDeposit and expeditedMinDeposit remove economic distinctions between normal and expedited proposals
body: In upgrades.go:103-104 , the setDefaultParams function constructs governance parameters using govtypesv1.NewParams . The first argument sets minDeposit to 1,000,000,000,000 untrn , and the second argument sets expeditedMinDeposit to the same value. This is incorrect because the x/gov module's ValidateBasic function requires that expeditedMinDeposit is strictly greater than minDeposit . During the upgrade, this validation is bypassed because Params.Set writes directly to the storage. Consequently, setting both deposits to the same amount removes the economic distinction between normal and expedited proposals. Expedited proposals are meant to carry a higher deposit cost to compensate for their shorter voting period (3 days vs 14 days). With identical 16 deposits, proposers can use the expedited path at no additional cost, undermining the governance design that trades higher financial commitment for faster resolution. Recommendation We recommend setting expeditedMinDeposit to a value greater than minDeposit . For example, the SDK default uses a 5x multiplier . Status: Resolved

title: Incomplete fund migration leading to permanent token lock in deprecated module accounts
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:410-437 , the BurnFunds migration function only sweeps and burns funds from the revenue-treasury module account and a hardcoded staking rewards contract address, while failing to handle other legacy module accounts associated with the deprecated revenue and feeburner modules. Specifically, the revenue-fee-redistribute and revenue-staking-rewards module accounts are not checked or processed during the upgrade. If any non-zero balance exists in these accounts, due to prior logic errors, failed executions, misconfigurations, or direct token transfers, those funds will remain stranded after the upgrade. Since the corresponding modules and their storage are removed, no remaining module retains the permissions or logic required to access or transfer these funds. This creates a permanent loss-of-funds scenario where tokens remain locked at the account level but are irrecoverable through standard protocol mechanisms. Recommendation We recommend extending the migration logic to explicitly query and handle all legacy module accounts, including revenue-fee-redistribute and revenue-staking-rewards . Status: Resolved

title: 100% minInitialDepositRatio creates high entry barriers and renders deposit periods meaningless
body: In upgrades.go:112 , the minInitialDepositRatio governance parameter is set to math.LegacyOneDec() , which is 100%. This means the proposer must deposit the full 17 minDeposit (1,000,000,000,000 untrn, approximately $5,808 at current prices) when creating the proposal. This is problematic because the standard governance flow allows proposers to submit a proposal with a partial deposit, and then the community can contribute additional funds during the deposit period to meet the threshold. Consequently, setting the ratio to 100% renders the deposit period useless, as the full amount must be provided upfront. This creates a high financial barrier to creating proposals and removes the community's ability to signal support by co-funding them. Recommendation We recommend lowering minInitialDepositRatio to a level that enables community participation during the deposit phase. Alternatively, if full upfront deposits are intended, consider documenting this as a deliberate design decision and shortening the deposit period accordingly. Status: Acknowledged

title: Zero proposalCancelRatio enables costless governance spam
body: In upgrades.go:113 , the proposalCancelRatio governance parameter is set to math.LegacyZeroDec() , which is 0%. This is problematic because the parameter controls the fraction of the deposit burned when a proposer cancels their own proposal. With a 0% cancellation ratio, a proposer can create a proposal, have it appear on governance dashboards to attract community attention, then cancel it without losing any of their deposit. Consequently, this enables low-cost signaling attacks: an actor could repeatedly submit misleading or controversial proposals to influence market sentiment or governance discussions, cancelling them before a vote concludes. The actor does not lose anything as the deposit is fully refunded each time. Recommendation We recommend setting proposalCancelRatio to a non-zero value (e.g., the SDK default of 50% ) to impose a cost on proposal cancellation. Status: Acknowledged 18

title: PuppeteerAdmin retains migration permission post-upgrade
body: In upgrades.go:272-287 , the MigratePuppeteer function migrates the Puppeteer contract to a new proxy contract code. The migration message uses PuppeteerAdmin as the sender, which is the Puppeteer contract's migration admin. However, after the migration completes, PuppeteerAdmin remains the migration admin. This means PuppeteerAdmin can call MigrateContract again at any time after the upgrade, migrating the Puppeteer contract to arbitrary code. Recommendation We recommend clearing the contract admin after migration by calling MsgClearAdmin . Alternatively, if continued admin access is intentional, consider documenting this as a design decision. Status: Resolved

title: Truncated redelegation amounts diverge from internal accounting, leaving new validators underfunded
body: In upgrades.go:544 , calcRedelegations constructs MsgBeginRedelegate messages with Amount: sdk.NewCoin(denom, take.TruncateInt()) , which truncates the fractional take value to an integer. However, in line 547 , the internal Redelegated tracker is updated with the untruncated value: redelegations[newValIdx].Redelegated = redelegations[newValIdx].Redelegated.Add(take) . This creates a growing discrepancy between what the algorithm thinks it has delegated and what the SDK actually moves. For example, if take is 33.33 across three messages, Redelegated accumulates to 99.99 while only 99 tokens (33 + 33 + 33) are actually redelegated. The needed calculation in line 527 uses the inflated Redelegated sum, causing the algorithm to consider a validator "full" before it has actually received its target amount. Consequently, new validators end up underfunded by the cumulative truncation error. 19 Recommendation We recommend using the truncated integer value consistently for both the message amount and the internal Redelegated tracker. This ensures the algorithm's accounting matches the actual tokens moved by the SDK. Status: Resolved

title: Zero-amount redelegation messages from TruncateInt halt the upgrade
body: In upgrades.go:544 , take.TruncateInt() is used as the coin amount in MsgBeginRedelegate . The take value is computed as min(remaining, needed) in lines 531-536 , where both remaining and needed are values derived from fractional share arithmetic. The issue is that if take is less than 1 (e.g., 0.5 shares remaining after prior iterations), TruncateInt evaluates it to 0. The SDK's BeginRedelegate message server checks !msg.Amount.Amount.IsPositive() before any further processing, rejecting the message with an ErrInvalidRequest error. Since RedelegateDaoFunds does not handle this error gracefully, the upgrade handler aborts. Recommendation Consider converting shares to integer token amounts before the redistribution loop to eliminate fractional arithmetic entirely. Status: Resolved

title: setDefaultParams name misrepresents scope
body: In upgrades.go:100-196 , the setDefaultParams function is documented as setting "default parameters for gov, mint, and distribution modules". However, in practice, it executes the entire upgrade logic beyond parameter configuration, such as initializing distribution state from staking, changing IBC rate-limit roles, and configuring the fee market. Recommendation We recommend renaming the function to accurately reflect its scope, such as executeUpgradeSteps . Status: Resolved 20

title: BurnFunds error prints module name instead of address
body: In upgrades.go:413 , the error message for a zero-balance revenue treasury uses the %s string placeholder for RevenueModuleAccount , which is the module name constant "revenue-treasury" . This produces an error like " revenue treasury revenue-treasury balance is not expected to be zero ", which provides no actionable information for debugging. Recommendation We recommend changing the error format to include the derived module address: authtypes.NewModuleAddress(RevenueModuleAccount) . Status: Resolved

title: removeSchedule error references removed admin module
body: In wasmbinding/message_plugin.go:861 , the error message for unauthorized removeSchedule calls reads " only admin or security dao can remove schedule ". However, the admin module has been removed as part of the upgrade, so only the security DAO address is checked in line 860 . The error message is misleading because it suggests admin module authorization still exists. Recommendation We recommend updating the error message to " only the security dao can remove schedule " to accurately reflect the current authorization logic. Status: Resolved

title: Stale comment incorrectly states that GovMsg::VoteWeighted does not work with Neutron
body: In app/app.go:793-794 , a comment states that the cosmwasm_1_2 capability enables GovMsg::VoteWeighted , which does not work with Neutron because it uses its own custom governance. Since this PR migrates Neutron to the native Cosmos SDK gov module, GovMsg::VoteWeighted may now work as expected and the comment no longer reflects the current state of the codebase. 21 Recommendation We recommend verifying whether GovMsg::VoteWeighted works correctly with the new governance setup and, if so, removing or updating the comment accordingly. Status: Resolved

title: Multiple hardcoded values in the upgrade handler will cause deployment failure
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:51-69 , several constants required by the upgrade handler are left as placeholder values: ● NewMaxValidators = 1 ● PuppeteerAdmin = "TODO" (an invalid address used as the sender in MigratePuppeteer ) ● ProxyContractCodeID = 0x0000 (resolves to 0 , a non-existent code ID used in the same migration) ● UndelegationsManagerContract = "TODO" (an invalid address used as the cron schedule target in RegisterCronSchedules ) ● NewValidatorSet contains a single placeholder validator address with a TODO comment indicating it has not been finalized If deployed in this state, the upgrade handler will fail during execution. MigratePuppeteer will error on the invalid sender address or missing code ID, and RegisterCronSchedules will register a cron pointing at an invalid contract. Also, hard-coding the staking module's MaxValidators parameter to 1 forces the Tendermint consensus set to a single bonded validator and collapses the chain's security model from Byzantine fault tolerance to complete trust in one operator. Recommendation We recommend filling in all values with the correct production addresses and code IDs before deploying this upgrade, and adding a preflight validation at the start of CreateUpgradeHandler that asserts all constants are valid bech32 addresses and that ProxyContractCodeID is non-zero. Status: Acknowledged 22

title: SetupStaking writes staking params twice via two different code paths
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:447-459 , SetupStaking first writes the updated MaxValidators directly to the store via sk.SetParams , then immediately re-writes the same params through stakingMsgServer.UpdateParams . The two calls are redundant: if SetParams succeeds, UpdateParams will also succeed and overwrite the same data. Recommendation We recommend removing the direct sk.SetParams call and relying solely on stakingMsgServer.UpdateParams , or vice versa, to avoid the redundant double write. Status: Resolved

title: BurnFunds fails hard if either account balance is zero at upgrade time
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:412-422 , BurnFunds returns an error if the revenue treasury or the staking rewards contract holds a zero balance, causing the entire upgrade handler to abort. If either account is empty at the upgrade block, the upgrade cannot complete. This makes the function sensitive to on-chain state at the time of upgrade scheduling. Recommendation We recommend replacing the hard failures with log warnings when a zero balance is encountered, allowing the upgrade to proceed gracefully. Alternatively, the expected balances should be verified in a dry-run against a mainnet state snapshot before the upgrade is scheduled. Status: Resolved 23

title: Transitive redelegation rule may block RedelegateDaoFunds if recent redelegations exist
body: In app/upgrades/nextupgrade/upgrades.go:486 , RedelegateDaoFunds calls BeginRedelegate for each Puppeteer delegation. The Cosmos SDK enforces a transitive redelegation prevention rule: if a delegator has an incoming redelegation to a given source validator that is still within the unbonding period (20 days on Neutron), a subsequent BeginRedelegate from that validator will fail with ErrTransitiveRedelegation , aborting the upgrade. We classify this issue as informational, as the Drop puppeteer contract has been verified on-chain to have no active redelegations at the time of this review. Recommendation We recommend verifying before scheduling the upgrade that no redelegations to any current Puppeteer source validator have occurred within the preceding 20 days. Consider adding a runtime check at the start of RedelegateDaoFunds that scans for active incoming redelegations and skips or logs affected validators rather than failing hard. Status: Acknowledged 24

title: Removing merchant does not remove associated deposit addresses
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/auth/merchant.rs:45-66 , the remove_merchant function does not remove the merchant's associated deposit addresses from the CUSTODIAN_DEPOSIT_ADDRESS_PER_MERCHANT and MERCHANT_DEPOSIT_ADDRESS storage. When a merchant is removed, they should no longer have the associated roles assigned. However, the GetCustodianDepositAddress and GetMerchantDepositAddress queries will show that the removed merchant still has a valid deposit address on the Bitcoin blockchain. Recommendation We recommend removing the merchant's deposit addresses from the CUSTODIAN_DEPOSIT_ADDRESS_PER_MERCHANT and MERCHANT_DEPOSIT_ADDRESS storage when executing the remove_merchant function. Status: Resolved

title: Approving mint requests does not ensure the requestor still holds the merchant role
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/contract.rs:149-189 , when approving a pending mint request, no validation ensures that the requester still holds the merchant role. For example, consider a scenario where the member manager revokes the merchant role post the issuance of a mint request. The mint requester, no longer holding the merchant role, should not be permitted to receive WBTC. However, due to a lack of validation when the custodian approves the mint request, the requester can still receive WBTC even though they no longer hold the merchant role. We classify this issue as minor because the custodian is considered a privileged and trusted role. Recommendation We recommend adding a validation step to ensure the requester still holds the merchant role before approving a mint request. Status: Resolved 11

title: Incorrect governor attribute value emitted
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/contract.rs:58 , the governor attribute value is emitted as info.sender . This is incorrect because the governor's address is set to msg.governor , causing off-chain event listeners and blockchain indexers to record incorrect data. Recommendation We recommend emitting the governor's address as the msg.governor value. Status: Resolved

title: Merchant deposit addresses are not ensured to be unique
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/tokenfactory/deposit_address.rs:67-9 1 , the set_custodian_deposit_address function does not ensure that the provided deposit_address is unique across merchants. This could lead to a custodian mistakenly assigning the same deposit_address to multiple merchants. A malicious merchant could exploit this if the custodian unsuspectingly assigns an existing address to the malicious merchant. The malicious merchant could then issue duplicate mint requests with a transaction identifier of the duplicate address. Assume the custodian sets the same deposit address for two merchants. The first merchant sends BTC to the deposit address. The second merchant did not make a deposit, but they took the first merchant's transaction identifier and issued a mint request for themselves. Since the deposit address for the second merchant matches the transaction identifier's receiver address, the custodian might approve this deceptive mint request. We classify this issue as minor because it requires a misconfiguration by the custodian, which is a privileged and trusted role. Recommendation We recommend implementing a mechanism to ensure each deposit_address given to merchants is unique. One possible solution is to create an extra storage field in the form of a Map<String , bool> . This would store the deposit address as the key. When setting the custodian's deposit address, the set_deposit_address function should load this map using the deposit address to verify if it has been previously used. If it has, the transaction should be reverted with an error message indicating a duplicate deposit address. Status: Resolved 12

title: Separation of privileged addresses is not enforced
body: While extensive effort has been made to define privileged access roles within the protocol, privilege separation of these roles is not properly enforced. Currently, no validation exists to enforce that these privileges are designated to unique addresses. In the unlikely case of a compromised account, privilege sharing will have severe implications. While this measure cannot prevent account compromise, it can limit the impact and serve as an additional layer of security for the protocol. Another step that can be taken to reduce the impact of a compromised account is to implement timelocks to prevent frequent updates of addresses. Recommendation We recommend adding validation to prevent privileged address reuse and consider implementing timelocks following the update of these privileged addresses. Status: Resolved

title: Attributes are not properly emitted during contract instantiation
body: During the contract instantiation process, the initialize_governor function in contracts/wbtc-controller/src/auth/governor.rs:16 returns attributes, but they are not used by the calling function in contracts/wbtc-controller/src/contract.rs:44 . Consequently, the attributes will not be properly emitted during instantiation. Recommendation We recommend adding these attributes to the response of the instantiate function. Status: Resolved

title: GetMintRequestsCount and GetBurnRequestsCount query fails when there are no mint or burn requests
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/tokenfactory/nonce.rs:30-33 , the custom get function returns the stored nonce value in the storage using the load function. Since the load function fails when there is no previously stored value, the 13 GetMintRequestsCount and GetBurnRequestsCount queries will fail when no mint or burn requests are issued. Recommendation We recommend using unwrap_or_default() so the query defaults to 0 instead of failing. Status: Resolved

title: Contracts should implement a two-step ownership transfer
body: The contracts within the scope of this audit allow the current owner to execute a one-step ownership transfer. While this is common practice, it presents a risk for the ownership of the contract to become lost if the owner transfers ownership to the incorrect address. A two-step ownership transfer will allow the current owner to propose a new owner, and then the account that is proposed as the new owner may call a function that will allow them to claim ownership and actually execute the config update. Recommendation We recommend implementing a two-step ownership transfer. The flow can be as follows:

title: The current owner proposes a new owner address that is validated. 2. The new owner account claims ownership, which applies the configuration changes. Status: Resolved 9. Typographical error affects codebase readability
body: In contracts/wbtc-controller/src/tokenfactory/deposit_address.rs:12 , the wrongly typed DepositAddressMananger occurs, which should be DepositAddressManager . While the typography error doesn't affect the code functionality, it increases the chances of introducing mistakes that can be easily avoided. Recommendation We recommend correcting the typographic error as described above. Status: Resolved 14

title: Storage entries spread across multiple files increase the chances of storage key collision
body: The contract contains multiple storage entries that are defined in separate files. While this does not affect the code quality, it increases the likelihood of accidental storage key collisions. One common pattern is consolidating all storage entries into a single file, increasing code readability and reducing the likelihood of storage key collisions. Recommendation We recommend consolidating all storage entries into a single file. Status: Resolved 15 Threat Model Analysis Methodology Process Applied The process performed to analyze the system for potential threats and build a comprehensive model is based on the approach first pioneered by Microsoft in 1999 that has developed into the STRIDE model ( https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/commerce-server/ee823878(v=cs.20) . Whilst STRIDE is aimed at traditional software systems, it is generic enough to provide a threat classification suitable for blockchain applications with little adaptation (see below). The result of the STRIDE classification has then been applied to a risk management matrix with simple countermeasures and mitigations suitable for blockchain applications. STRIDE Interpretation in the Blockchain Context STRIDE was first designed for closed software applications in permissioned environments with limited network capabilities. However, the classification provided can be adapted to blockchain systems with small adaptations. The below table highlights a blockchain-centric interpretation of the STRIDE classification: Spoofing In a blockchain context, the authenticity of communications is built into the underlying cryptographic public key infrastructure. However, spoofing attack vectors can occur at the off-chain level and within a social engineering paradigm. An example of the former is a Sybil attack where an actor uses multiple cryptographic entities to manipulate a system (wash-trading, auction smart contract manipulation, etc.). The latter usually consists of attackers imitating well-known actors, for instance, the creation of an impersonation token smart contract with a malicious implementation. Tampering Similarly to spoofing, tampering of data is usually not directly relevant to blockchain data itself due to cryptographic integrity. One example of this is a supply chain attack that manages to inject malicious code or substitute trusted software that interacts with the blockchain (node software, wallets, libraries). Repudiation Repudiation, i.e. the ability of an actor to deny that they have taken action is usually not relevant at the transaction level of blockchains. However, it makes 16 sense to maintain this category, since it may apply to additional software used in blockchain applications, such as user-facing web services. An example is the claim of a loss of a private key and hence assets. Information Disclosure Information disclosure has to be treated differently at the blockchain layer and the off-chain layer. Since the blockchain state is inherently public in most systems, information leakage here relates to data that is discoverable on the blockchain, even if it should be protected. Predictable random number generation could be classified as such, in addition to simply storing private data on the blockchain. In some cases, information in the mempool (pending/unconfirmed transactions) can be exploited in front-running or sandwich attacks. At the off-chain layer, the leakage of private keys is a good example of operational threat vectors. Denial of Service Denial of service threat vectors translates directly to blockchain systems at the infrastructure level. At the smart contract or protocol layer, there are more subtle DoS threats, such as unbounded iterations over data structures that could be exploited to make certain transactions not executable. Elevated Privileges Elevated privilege attack vectors directly translate to blockchain services. Faulty authorization at the smart contract level is only one example where users might obtain access to functionality that should not be accessible. 17 Assets The following describes assets that may be valuable to an attacker or other stakeholders of the system. Privileged roles The defined messages in the contract can only be executed from privileged roles: the governor, member manager, custodian, and merchants. These accounts present an attractive target for attackers because each role is authorized to execute messages that may affect the circulating supply of WBTC tokens. WBTC token The WBTC token is created from the x/tokenfactory module, which is backed by Bitcoin on the Bitcoin blockchain. It is a native token type that holds the equivalent value of a BTC token, and it can be traded on the market, such as decentralized exchanges, or extract value in various ways, making it an attractive target for attackers. Custody wallet BitGo holds BTC in a custody wallet and acts as backing for WBTC minted by protocol. The WBTC/BTC peg relies on the security of this wallet. If an attacker managed to gain access to it and steal funds, the invariant that 1 BTC always backs 1 WBTC would no longer hold, causing WBTC to lose value. Modules of the underlying blockchain The architecture of the protocol relies on the x/bank and x/tokenfactory modules of the Osmosis chain. The former manages the circulating token supply as well as transfers, while the latter handles authentication for minting and burning WBTC. These modules are an attractive target to attackers as an unexpected vulnerability might allow them to mint, burn or take possession of WBTC tokens. Private keys controlling external accounts In the case of externally owned accounts, some entity holds a private key in the control of that account. An attacker finds access to a private key valuable since that gives them full control over the account, allowing them to impersonate and act on behalf of the account owner. Migration authorization In CosmWasm smart contracts, if there is a defined contract admin, the contract is not immutable. Gaining unauthorized access to act as the contract admin is valuable to an attacker, as it allows them to modify the contract's source code, potentially introducing backdoors or other malicious code. 18 Liveness of the protocol An attacker may find it valuable to target the liveness of the protocol, such as preventing the minting and burning of WBTC tokens. This could allow the attackers to disrupt issuing of new tokens, delay trading, prevent tokens from being burned, or extort stakeholders to stop the attack. Liveness of the underlying blockchains Attacking the liveness of underlying blockchains can also be valuable to an attacker. By doing so, they may profit from shorting the tokens or extorting stakeholders to stop the attack, causing disruptions and instability in the blockchain ecosystem. Osmosis block times are dependent on the validator set coming to a consensus. Several factors may impact this, such as consensus failures that stem from building a block or issues that stem from the ABCI operations that may slow or halt the chain. Blockchain light nodes Many actors choose not to run a full blockchain node, mainly due to its resource demands. As an alternative, they may run a light node and rely on other full nodes to obtain relevant information. The custodian might opt for such a light node to determine whether BTC was deposited successfully to the merchant deposit address. Unlike full nodes, light nodes do not validate whether all transactions comply with Bitcoin's consensus rules. Instead, the connected full nodes are trusted to validate them. Due to that, light clients are vulnerable to Eclipse attacks, where an attacker that controls all connected nodes is able to feed misinformation to the light node, particularly transactions that do not adhere to the consensus rules. For example, spending a transaction output twice can lead to the issuance of unbacked WBTC. For this attack to be successful, the attacker would need to mine the block with the double-spend and then mine enough blocks to meet the confirmation thresholds of the custodian. While this is quite expensive in practice on the Bitcoin blockchain, it might be economically viable. Blockchain consensus Blockchain consensus protocols establish agreement among network participants regarding transaction validity and order, ensuring trust and security within the network. Suppose an attacker gains control over the Bitcoin network's consensus via a 51% attack or the Cosmos SDK chain (either by compromising validator nodes or coordinating collusion). In that case, the integrity of the WBTC protocol could be compromised. The economic feasibility of such an attack grows as the total value locked in the protocol increases. This is problematic especially if one of the chains has a relatively low market capitalization/low staking ratio. 19 Stakeholders/Potential Threat Actors WBTC token holders The main users of the protocol transact with WBTC tokens, which they can exchange,

title: Lack of denom validation
body: Upon instantiation, the transmuter contract creates a pool with multiple denoms through the TransmuterPool::new function. However, the supplied denoms are not effectively validated in contracts/transmuter/src/transmuter_pool/mod.rs:16-24 . Incorrect denominations or an input typo would render some of the contract's features unusable, requiring a new instantiation and for the users to withdraw current deposits. Recommendation We recommend querying each denomination before storing it to ensure that the supplied string is a valid denomination, for example, by checking its metadata. Status: Resolved

title: Missing validation steps when registering limiters
body: The transmuter contract lacks validation on some of the functions related to limiters. Neither upper_limit nor boundary_offset undergo any validation when newly created in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:63-64 and 207-209 or when updated in lines 314 and 348 . If a value of zero is provided, most trades will fail to satisfy the limiter's restrictions, making some features unusable. On the other hand, if a large number is set, the contract could become rapidly imbalanced as described in the issue Lack of limiters could result in uncontrolled pool imbalance The label field is allowed to be empty upon registration of a new limiter in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:287 . Although not a security risk, it can be misleading and affect the user experience. Finally, when registering a new limiter the target denomination is not checked to be part of the current pool in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:286-288 . This will render the limiter ineffective in case of a mistake or a typo, leaving the intended denomination without any control against imbalance. 10 Recommendation We recommend validating both upper_limit and boundary_offset to be greater than zero and below a reasonable amount that effectively limits arbitrage. In addition, we recommend validating that the trimmed label field is not an empty string. We also recommend validating that the denom of each new limiter is part of the pool assets. Status: Partially Resolved The client stated that they lacked data to decide on a reasonable upper limit and prefer to experiment without placing constraints that could make the pool unusable. The rest of the recommendations have been implemented.

title: Unbounded loops could render main features unusable
body: The transmuter contract includes a nested for loop structure in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:391-394 . The outer loop iterates through all denominations specified during pool initialization while the inner loop iterates through all limiters registered by the admin. The size of both vectors can be arbitrarily decided by the admin. If any of these vectors is excessively large, it can significantly inflate the gas cost for swap operations, pool joins, or exits, potentially causing operations to revert. The risk escalates when both arrays are overly extended, due to the quadratic computational complexity. Although the comments in lines 365 and 378 state that the number of limiters is expected to be small, no actual mechanism is found to prevent the described scenario. Recommendation We recommend limiting the maximum number of limiters per denomination and denominations per pool. Status: Resolved

title: Zero-value swaps are allowed and introduce inefficiencies
body: contracts/transmuter/src/sudo.rs defines the SwapExactAmountIn and SwapExactAmountOut messages which are used by the Pool Manager module of Osmosis to automatically execute swaps, including multi-hop swaps. 11 These messages contain the token_in and token_out Coin fields. If any of the Coin fields have an amount field set to zero, unnecessary swaps are performed. Unnecessary steps in a multi-hop swap could cause excessive gas costs for a user who might not be aware of the transmuter pool being used. For example, the SudoMsg::SwapExactAmountIn message triggers such a redundant swap when token_in is set to Coin::new(0, "ABC".to_string()) and token_out_min_amount is set to Uint128::from(0) . Similarly, the SudoMsg::SwapExactAmountOut message will cause redundant swaps for any valid token_in_max_amount if token_out is set to a value such as Coin::new(0, "XYZ".to_string()). These messages can be sent from the Pool Manager module automatically as part of a bigger swap route. For example, redundant parameter combinations from the out-of-scope cosmwasmpool implementation could cause this issue. Recommendation We recommend validating that the input and output amounts are not zero before executing a swap. Status: Resolved

title: Unoptimized zero amount burning or minting
body: The functions swap_tokens_for_alloyed_asset and swap_alloyed_asset_for_tokens , defined in contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:299 and 370 , allow minting or burning of zero alloyed tokens. These scenarios arise from join_pool and exit_pool entry points when a user passes a Coin structure with an amount set to zero. Although the resulting submessage to x/bank module will fail, unnecessary computation and hence gas will be spent as both functions call check_limits_and_update which can be computationally intensive due to nested iterations inside. Recommendation We recommend validating that the amounts to mint or burn are not zero as early as possible to increase efficiency. Status: Resolved 12

title: Deregistering of non-existing limiters silently fails
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:187 , during limiter deregistration, the deregister function declared in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:290 is called. It performs removal operations over the vector without any prior validation, taking denom and label as parameters. The returned value of this operation is the same when an element is removed from the vector and when there is no match. As a consequence, users will receive identical output for existing and non-existing (denom, label) pairs. This could lead to situations where limiters intended to be removed but containing a typo may still be in place after the admin tries to remove them. Recommendation We recommend checking that the provided (denom, label) pair is part of the limiters in storage, raising an error if that is not the case. Status: Resolved

title: Missing Division invariant check
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/division.rs , the Division structure is declared to carry two timestamps: started_at denoting the beginning of the span, and updated_at denoting the last modification time of the division's value. Line 49 enforces that updated_at is not before started_at . However, it does not enforce that updated_at is not after the division's end which is defined as started_at + division_size . This missing invariant check makes reasoning about divisions more difficult. Recommendation We recommend enforcing updated_at <= started_at + division_size since only divisions adjacent to new blocks can be updated, not previous ones. Status: Resolved 13

title: Admin transfer procedure can be enhanced
body: contracts/transmuter/src/admin.rs implements a two-step admin transfer pattern following best practices, requiring the receiving side to accept ownership via the claim function. However, there is no dedicated API to cancel a proposed transfer. At present, the current contract admin can only cancel an unclaimed admin transfer by directing the privileges back to their own address, followed by claiming this mock transfer, which is inefficient. Recommendation We recommend creating a dedicated entry point to allow the cancellation of an admin privilege transfer and rejecting transfers to the current owner address. Status: Resolved

title: Redundant query function
body: The transmuter contract includes two queriable functions that are effectively identical: get_share_denom in contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:499 and get_alloyed_denom in line 510 . Although not a security issue, having redundant code is unnecessary and can decrease maintainability. Recommendation We recommend removing one of these redundant functions. Status: Resolved

title: Lack of limiters could result in uncontrolled pool imbalance
body: The transmuter contract enforces a 1-1 relation between its pool assets. The limiter feature is in place to avoid swift liquidity imbalances happening when specific market conditions open arbitrage opportunities. However, there is no minimum amount of limiters required. Upon instantiation, no limiter is created, which could be intended to facilitate a fast initial liquidity provision. From that on, the lack of a limiter, or a malicious admin removing all the limiters through the deregister_limiter function in 14 contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:120-190 , open up unlimited arbitrage opportunities that may imbalance the pools to an undesirable level. Recommendation We recommend that after a reasonable amount of liquidity has been reached, corresponding to the initial fast liquidity provision, no more liquidity is accepted until a minimum of one limiter per denom is set. In addition, a minimum of one limiter per asset in the pool should be enforced when the admin removes limiters. Status: Partially Resolved The client stated that they lacked data to set a fixed liquidity cap to enforce the first batch of limiters. They choose to experiment with flexibility on when to set the initial limiters. Our recommendation to enforce a minimum of one limiter when modifying limiters has been implemented.

title: Lack of role-based access controls for the pausing mechanism
body: The codebase implements a pausing mechanism, which is in line with best practices. However, all of the administrative functions of the contract are centralized in the admin role, which goes against the principle of least privilege. Segregating the pauser role has the additional benefit of swifter reactions in case of need when assigned to an EOA compared to the admin that might be managed by a multisig or a governance contract. Recommendation We recommend implementing a separate pauser role that can turn on and off the pausing mechanism. Status: Resolved

title: Default value conceals unexpected state
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/division.rs : 310-316 , the compressed_moving_average function manages cases where result computation is 15 infeasible. This arises when the time span in focus has a length of zero, occurring when block time matches the start time of the earliest division remaining post-pruning. However, such a division must not exist since the average is computed prior to the division set update. The function currently defaults to returning zero, masking a potential issue with division updates. While this is not a security concern, maintaining an accurate state aids in the early identification and resolution of any unexpected states. Recommendation We recommend throwing an error instead of returning the default value if an unexpected state is reached. Status: Resolved

title: Incorrect error message
body: The transmuter contract's exit_pool function checks if the provided token_out coins are part of the pool. If one of the assets is not part of the pool, it raises an incorrect InsufficientPoolAsset error instead of InvalidPoolAssetDenom . Although not a security risk, incorrect or non-descriptive errors may mislead users. Recommendation We recommend returning the appropriate error. Status: Resolved

title: Typographical error in attribute naming
body: The response for the transfer_admin entry point response carries attributes "method" and "andidate" , defined in contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs : 777-779 . Presumably, "candidate" was the intended name. Within CosmWasm, attributes play important roles in event logging, auditability, and interoperability. A typographical mistake might lead off-chain components or other modules to miss events. 16 Recommendation We recommend correcting typographical errors to improve readability. Status: Resolved

title: Unused error messages
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/error.rs , several error messages are defined but remain unused, specifically: ● InvalidPoolAssetDenom (see Incorrect error message ) ● FundsMismatchTokenIn Recommendation We recommend removing unused error messages to improve the maintainability of the codebase. Status: Resolved

title: Usage of panics for error handling
body: It has been noticed that the expect macro is used in contracts/transmuted/src/limiter/limiters.rs:154 for the error handling mechanism. The usage of expect is generally discouraged because it leads to panics without a developer-friendly error message. expect also causes the wasm execution to abort, which does not allow handling of the error from calling functions. Recommendation We recommend unifying the error handling mechanism in order to standardize individual parts of the code, which will increase readability and simplify the code development process in the future. Status: Resolved 17

title: Usage of vulnerable dependencies
body: It was found that the codebase uses dependencies utilizing packages with known vulnerabilities. As reported in https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2022-0093 and https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2023-0052 , the ed25519-dalek and webpki crates are affected by issues of high impact. These vulnerabilities are not directly exploitable in a CosmWasm smart contract and do not affect any of the current code fragments. Therefore this issue has been raised with informational severity for completeness. Recommendation We suggest verifying that the current code development process does not include any vulnerable dependencies, as well as periodically checking publicly known issues in the dependencies used. Status: Acknowledged 18

title: Corrupted assets may not be removed when liquidity reaches zero
body: The transmuter contract's specification states that corrupted assets should be removed from the contract when liquidity is zero. This is done when all the corrupted assets are redeemed at the same time in contracts/transmuter/src/swap.rs:267-276 , but not in any other cases such as pool exits and transmutes during unchecked_exit_pool in contracts/transmuter/src/transmuter_pool/exit_pool.rs:12-43 and update_pool_assets in contracts/transmuter/src/transmuter_pool/transmute.rs:38-75 . Note that the current implementation does not have any other way of removing corrupted assets from the pool. Recommendation We recommend checking if the liquidity of a corrupted asset has reached zero and, if so, removing it from the pool. Status: Resolved

title: Resetting change limiters creates an opportunity window for economic attacks
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:225-228 , the states of all change limiters are reset. This is done when new assets are added because weights are no longer correct and should be recalculated. However, change limiters implement protection from rapid market changes and pool imbalances. Removing them, even temporarily, creates an opportunity window for economic attacks. A malicious party capable of joining the pool with a large position can simply listen to the contract's on-chain events and deploy the attack as soon as new assets are added. Recommendation We recommend implementing a change limiters upgrade mechanism that would create a new division with a recalculated safe average for each existing asset. Status: Resolved 10

title: Incorrect spot price calculation
body: The spot_price function returns a fixed value of Decimal:one() in contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:673 . This is incorrect as the assets in the pool can have different normalization factors, resulting in prices other than 1. We classify this issue as minor because the affected function does not impact the logic of the contract, as it is exclusively used in a query. However, note that it could have a severe impact on external contracts relying on this information. This issue was independently reported by the Osmosis team during the audit. Recommendation We recommend taking the normalization factor of the assets into account to calculate the spot price. Status: Resolved

title: Outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities in use
body: The transmuter contract makes use of outdated libraries that contain known vulnerabilities. Although we did not find these vulnerabilities to be exploitable in the current codebase, updates to the codebase may lead to security risks in the future. The following libraries are affected: ● sylvia 0.7.0 ○ Affected by RUSTSEC-2024-0012 ● cosmwasm-std 1.3.1 ○ Affected by CWA-2024-002 Recommendation We recommend updating the affected crates to their latest version. Status: Resolved

title: Alloyed asset normalization factor lacks validation
body: The set_normalizaton_factor function in contracts/transmuter/src/alloyed_asset.rs:67-73 saves the normalization 11 factor for the alloyed asset. However, this value does not undergo any validation as opposed to the normalization factor of the pool assets. If, by mistake, a value of zero is assigned to the normalization factor of the alloyed asset the features that operate with the alloyed asset will error, making them unusable. Recommendation We recommend ensuring the normalization factor is greater than zero before saving it. Status: Resolved

title: ChangeLimiter missing validation upon update
body: The set_change_limiter_boundary_offset function in contracts/transmuter/src/limiter/limiters.rs:416-447 does not validate the boundary_offset value through ensure_boundary_offset_constrain before saving it. Recommendation We recommend ensuring the value is larger than zero before saving it. Status: Resolved

title: Migration lacks validation steps
body: The add_normalization_factor_to_pool_assets function in contracts/transmuter/src/migrations/v3_0_0.rs:67-73 and the set_alloyed_asset_normalization_factor function in lines 113-121 save the normalization factor for the alloyed asset and the pool assets upon migration. However, these values do not undergo any validation. If a value of zero is mistakenly assigned to the assets' normalization factor, most of the main features would become unusable. Recommendation We recommend ensuring that the normalization factors are greater than zero before saving them. Status: Resolved 12

title: Adminship can be renounced, leading to inability to maintain the protocol
body: The transmuter contract implements a renounce_adminship entry point in contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:776-785 , which leaves the contract without any address holding admin privileges. Given that several functions needed for the correct long-term operation of the contract are restricted to the admin address only, it will not be possible to maintain the protocol if the adminship is dropped at any point. We classify this issue as minor since it can only be caused by the admin, who is a trusted entity. Recommendation We recommend removing the renounce_adminship entry point. Status: Resolved

title: Outdated documentation
body: The transmuter contract restricts access to its set_active_status function to moderator users only, following security best practices. However, the access control table in the repository's README.md file incorrectly states that this function should be restricted to admin users only. Recommendation We recommend updating the documentation to reflect the current implementation. Status: Resolved

title: Instantiation without a moderator is allowed
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:81 , the transmuter contract instantiation is parameterized by an optional address for the moderator. The moderator role is responsible for pausing the contract if any security issue arises and marking assets as corrupt. There are other ways to pause the contract, either by governance or by the admin, but they are less straightforward and potentially slower to react. Specifically, 13 governance would need to pass the proposal, which takes time. On the other hand, the admin would need to grant itself moderator privileges first, and this is one more step that can count in critical scenarios. As a consequence, the contract would ideally not allow a configuration with the moderator set to None . Recommendation We recommend making the moderator field non-optional. During instantiation, either the deployer should explicitly specify the moderator address or a fallback could be implemented to set the moderator address to be equal to the admin address. Status: Resolved

title: Miscellaneous performance optimizations
body: The codebase contains minor inefficiencies that affect performance and hence gas costs: ● In contracts/transmuter/src/transmuter_pool/add_new_assets.rs:9- 10 , the assets vector is checked for duplicates first, and then its length is checked for being below the limit. However, duplicate search is a more computationally intensive operation and should be performed after the more efficient length check. ● In contracts/transmuter/src/transmuter_pool/corrupted_assets.rs: 91 , the pool_assets vector is iterated to discover any corrupted assets. If such has not been found, the control flow prematurely returns. Then, in lines 97-101 , the same vector is iterated again to filter corrupted assets and construct a HashMap . Redundant iteration could be avoided by performing the check between the filtering and creating the HashMap . ● In contracts/transmuter/src/swap.rs:431 , the code responsible for checking if token_out.denom differs from token_in.denom is not necessary as two lines later, during the execution of the swap_variant function, the same check is performed as well. ● In contracts/transmuter/src/swap.rs:498 , the code responsible for checking if token_out.denom differs from token_in.denom is not necessary, as two lines later, during the execution of the swap_variant function, the same check is performed as well. 14 Recommendation We recommend removing the inefficiencies described above. Status: Resolved

title: Missing current status validation during updates may mislead users
body: In contracts/transmuter/src/contract.rs:456 , the set_active_status function, as well as SetActive sudo message in contracts/transmuter/src/sudo.rs:48 , no validation ensures that the current and updated statuses are not equal. Consequently, even if these values are equal, information will be emitted stating that the status has been changed. This might be misleading and may even have a security impact on contract management during an incident. Recommendation We recommend ensuring that the current and updated values are not equal. Status: Resolved

title: Unused code
body: The codebase contains unused code, which may indicate that the logic has changed or that assumptions do not match the current implementation. Instances of unused code have been found as follows: ● SingleTokenExpected error in contracts/transmuter/src/error.rs:24 ● InvalidTokenInAmount error in contracts/transmuter/src/error.rs:80 ● UnexpectedDenom error in contracts/transmuter/src/error.rs:100 Recommendation We recommend using or removing unused code from the codebase. Status: Resolved 15
